However, filters or purifiers will not protect from high chemical concentrations or heavy metal contamination. It is best to avoid water sources such as mining tailing ponds or those near agricultural operations. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 55

Chapter 4 WATER PURIFICATION 4-81. Water should always be treated. No matter how clean the snow or water may appear, it should always be considered contaminated. There are many techniques to purify water, each with inherent advantages and disadvantages. 4-82. Boiling kills biological contaminants but does not eliminate chemical contaminants. Filtration should also be used if chemical contaminants are suspected. To ensure all biological contaminants have been killed, let the water boil for 1 minute. This method requires time and fuel while allowing water to be treated away from the source. 4-83. Chemical treatment can be accomplished with iodine or chlorine dioxide. These treatments are available commercially and come with instructions for proper use. Chemical treatment will kill almost all biological contaminants but are ineffective against cryptosporidium. It requires time for these chemical treatments to be effective, and, in cold temperatures, it takes longer. This method allows water to be treated away from the source and on the go. 4-84. UV lights are an effective way to kill all biological contaminants but do not treat for chemical contaminants. They require batteries and in cloudy debris-filled water, it may not kill all contaminants. Ensure water is filtered if it is cloudy

UV lights are an effective way to kill all biological contaminants but do not treat for chemical contaminants. They require batteries and in cloudy debris-filled water, it may not kill all contaminants. Ensure water is filtered if it is cloudy before use. This method can be used away from the source. 4-85. Filters are compact and lightweight. They work by filtering out particulate, chemicals, and biological contaminants. Filters are not capable of removing any chemical contaminants that are dissolved in the water. Certain filters may not be able to filter out smaller biological contaminants as the pores of the filter are too large to remove them. These types of filters are designed to remove waterborne protozoa and bacteria but not viruses. The benefit of these types of filters is that water moves more rapidly through them. Filters that can filter smaller contaminants are often referred to as water purifiers. Water purifiers are designed to remove protozoa, bacteria, and viruses, offering a higher level of defense by combating all three. The drawback to these types of filters is that they filter water at a slower rate and may clog when filtering very cloudy water. Be sure to read the capabilities of

In extreme temperatures, they may not operate at all. Filters require treating water at the source. AERIAL RESUPPLY 4-86. Movement of supplies by air is often the preferred method for remote, hard to reach locations. This is only possible when assets are available and the weather, terrain, and situation allow it. Chapter 5 Avalanche World War I is remembered for the brutal fighting in the trenches in France and Belgium. However, in the fighting between Italy and the Austro-Hungarian Empire, Soldiers saw some of the most intense mountain fighting in human history. After the Italians checked the Austrian offensive through the passes of the Alps, both sides fought higher and higher into the mountains. Small, light units of mountaineers clashed over new ground high in the peaks, while the armies dug in on the peaks they had secured. Positions and paths were blasted out of the rock and carved through the glaciers to move personnel and materiel to the fighting in the heights. By the winter of 1916, the line had mostly stabilized, and both armies were hunkering down for winter. Both sides had established extensive networks of trails and camps to support their forward positions; however, much of the infrastructure had been built in avalanche paths. In the second week of December, a major snowstorm blew in, loading the slopes and causing massive avalanches across the range. Both nations suppressed the number of casualties they received, and no official Italian records exist, but what evidence did survive paints a grim

of December, a major snowstorm blew in, loading the slopes and causing massive avalanches across the range. Both nations suppressed the number of casualties they received, and no official Italian records exist, but what evidence did survive paints a grim picture. The lowest estimates place casualties at around 4,000 during the storm. Some records support numbers as high as 10,000. Today, their bodies are still melting out of the glaciers below. SECTION I - AVALANCHE HAZARDS 5-1. During winter months and throughout the year, snow covers the slopes. Steep, snow-covered terrain, in addition to mobility challenges and fall hazards, present the risk of avalanches. This hazard is easy to underestimate. It is not clearly visible, and, due to the complexity of the factors involved, there is a high degree of uncertainty, but the consequences of ignoring the hazard are high. Avalanches have taken the lives of more troops engaged in mountain warfare than all other terrain hazards combined. 5-2. An avalanche is an unstable snowpack, located on particularly angled terrain, where the bonds between layers or several layers of snow have broken, causing a mass of snow to slide downhill. When operating in the mountains during the winter, these instabilities

avalanche is an unstable snowpack, located on particularly angled terrain, where the bonds between layers or several layers of snow have broken, causing a mass of snow to slide downhill. When operating in the mountains during the winter, these instabilities in the snowpack may make large areas too dangerous for travel. These snow slopes may appear unthreatening but may have weak layers buried in the snowpack that can be easily triggered. Military elements may gravitate into avalanche terrain to avoid steeper technical terrain or enemy observation. Avalanches can generate incredible destructive force, destroying equipment, killing or burying Soldiers, and blocking key roads. Whether operating dismounted in high alpine terrain or as a mounted force in valley bottoms, units must be aware of avalanche hazards. They must incorporate the evaluation of avalanche danger into the planning process and learn to recognize and avoid hazardous terrain. (See figure 5-1, page 64.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 63

Chapter 5 Figure 5-1. Movement through avalanche terrain AVALANCHE ELEMENTS 5-3. Avalanches occur when the weight of accumulated snow on a slope exceeds the cohesive forces that hold the snow in place. There are three elements needed to create an avalanche: an unstable snowpack, terrain steep enough to slide, and a trigger that initiates the failure of bonds holding the snow in place. SNOWPACK 5-4. Layers of snow accumulate with each new snow or wind event. Variation in temperature and atmospheric conditions form layers with different types of snow crystals. These layers are subject to changes in texture and strength throughout the winter, as they are exposed to sun, wind, and temperature changes. Each layer in the snowpack will have distinct characteristics. Strong layers are made up of well-bonded, small, rounded grains. Weak layers are made up of larger, angular, poorly bonded grains. Snowpack Concerns 5-5. Instabilities are weaknesses within the snowpack as described below (see figure 5-2): * Weak layers-weak layers may collapse under load, initiating an avalanche. Poorly bonded crystals can act like ball bearings between stronger layers. Weak layers can change over time, becoming stronger, denser layers. This happens more quickly in temperatures above freezing. However, many

However, many avalanche cycles are due to weak layers that resist this change and retain their large grain size and 64 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Avalanche * * angular shape for long periods. These types of layers are known as "persistent" weak layers. These are common in prolonged colder temperatures. Weak bonds between layers-differences in the size and compositions of crystals between layers inhibit bonding. Large differences between layers are the primary source of instability. Bed surface-the bed surface is the surface over which a fracture and subsequent avalanche release occurs. Smooth, uniform sliding surfaces provide less friction to hold the snow in place. Examples are firm old snow layers, rain crusts, and sun crusts. Figure 5-2. Snowpack layers Loading 5-6. When instability exists in the snowpack, another important factor is the load placed on top of the weak layer. With the added weight of accumulated snow, it increases the shear forces within the snowpack: * New snow-during snowstorms, snowfall will rapidly increase the forces placed on the snowpack. Snowfall of more than 2.5 centimeters (cm) (1 inch) of snow an hour or more than 30 cm (1 foot) of snow in 24 hours is considered critical loading. Avoid traveling in avalanche terrain during critical loading. * Wind loading-sustained winds will transport snow from windward slopes and ridge tops, depositing it in sheltered features on

30 cm (1 foot) of snow in 24 hours is considered critical loading. Avoid traveling in avalanche terrain during critical loading. * Wind loading-sustained winds will transport snow from windward slopes and ridge tops, depositing it in sheltered features on leeward aspects. With high winds, even small deposits of new snow can produce significant loading. Top loading occurs when wind deposits snow over the top of a ridge. Side loading (or cross loading) occurs when snow is blown across the slope and deposited in gullies or on the leeward sides of ridges. * Rain-rain rapidly increases the load on the snowpack and erodes bonds between snow crystals and layers. After a period of sustained cold where weak layers have been preserved in the snowpack, rain can produce dense, wet avalanches that are very destructive. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 65

Chapter 5 TERRAIN FACTORS 5-7. Terrain is the second factor that determines if an avalanche can occur. The character of a snowpack and opportunities for whether instabilities develop are determined by its elevation and aspect. A slope's characteristics-slope angle, shape, and physical characteristics-determine the likelihood of a slide. Recognizing and avoiding avalanche terrain are the keys to managing avalanche risk. Elevation 5-8. Precipitation, temperature, and wind often vary significantly at different elevations. This results in differences in the snowpack, all of which influence the type, size, distribution, and sensitivity of avalanches. 5-9. Increased precipitation-as weather systems are lifted over mountains (orthographic lift), the air cools and can hold less moisture, causing additional precipitation at elevation. Increased precipitation causes increased loads on the snowpack. 5-10. Temperature-warming in the snowpack temporarily increases instability as bonds melt but improves stability when it re-freezes. Cooler temperatures at higher elevations inhibit stabilization. Instabilities can persist for much longer. Aspect to Wind 5-11. Sustained winds of 15 mph or higher transport snow from the windward aspect of the slope and deposit it in the form of wind slabs on the leeward slopes. Leeward slopes can accumulate three to five times the amount of snow that falls

15 mph or higher transport snow from the windward aspect of the slope and deposit it in the form of wind slabs on the leeward slopes. Leeward slopes can accumulate three to five times the amount of snow that falls in sheltered locations. Slopes on the windward side have much of their new snow "scoured" off by the wind and are generally more stable than leeward slopes. Leeward slopes tend to form dangerous cornices and large, unstable slabs of snow. Aspect to Sun 5-12. Solar radiation causes drastic temperature swings in the snowpack. South-facing slopes can be dangerous on warm, sunny days immediately following storms. However, over time, these slopes stabilize as the added heat promotes bonding between layers. Snow on north-facing slopes does not stabilize as quickly and is more hazardous through most of the winter. Note. This effect is reversed in the Southern Hemisphere. Start Zone Characteristics 5-13. Terrain traps are features that increase the consequences of being caught in an avalanche. Examples include cliffs, gullies, creeks, lakes, trees, benches, or roads where debris will pile up, crevasses, or bergschrunds. Some terrain traps increase trauma during an avalanche. Others increase burial depth, making survival more unlikely. TRIGGERS 5-16. All avalanche triggers, whether caused by natural forces or human actions, are due to overloading the cohesive strength of the snowpack: * Natural-avalanches may be triggered by new snow, falling rock, snow, ice, or smaller avalanches. Solar warming erodes bonds and can trigger avalanches. Naturally occurring avalanches are a critical warning sign that the conditions for an avalanche exist on similar slopes. If natural avalanches are possible, human triggered avalanches are likely. * Human-most victims trigger the avalanches that kill them. People apply significant force to the snowpack.

Avalanches can be categorized into two broad categories: loose snow and slab avalanches. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) Loose snow slides start with less snow and pick up more snow as they descend. Slab avalanches occur when one or more layers of cohesive snow break away as a unit and are generally more destructive. 68 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Avalanche 5-18. There are many variations of these types, each with distinct characteristics. These characteristics are defined by the structures within the snowpack, how an avalanche is released, and where it is found in the terrain. These avalanche problems guide group discussions, route planning, terrain choices, and the observations made during snowpack evaluation. LOOSE-DRY AVALANCHES 5-19. A loose-dry avalanche is a release of dry, unconsolidated snow. These avalanches occur within layers of soft snow near the surface of the snowpack. Loose-dry avalanches start at a point and entrain snow as they move downhill, forming a fan-shaped avalanche. Other names for loose-dry avalanches include point-release avalanches or sluffs. Loose-dry avalanches can trigger slab avalanches that break into deeper snow layers. Loose-dry avalanches are usually less dangerous than other avalanche problems but can be hazardous when combined with terrain traps, such as gullies, rocks, dense timber, cliffs, or crevasses. (See figure 5-5, page 70.) STORM SLAB AVALANCHES 5-20. A storm slab avalanche is a release of a soft cohesive layer (a slab) of new snow that breaks within the storm snow or on the old snow surface. Storm-slab problems last between a few hours and a few days but often stabilize quickly.

A wind slab avalanche is the release of a cohesive layer of snow (a slab) formed by the wind. Wind transports snow from the upwind sides of terrain features and deposits snow on the downwind side. Wind slabs are often smooth and rounded, sound hollow sometimes, and can range from soft to hard. Wind slabs form in specific areas and are confined to lee and cross-loaded terrain features. A persistent slab avalanche is a release of a cohesive layer of soft to hard snow (a slab) in the middle to upper snowpack, when the bond to an underlying persistent weak layer breaks. More than any other hazard faced in the mountains, avalanches pose the most significant threat of a catastrophic accident for an entire element. In the planning phase, Soldiers should make every effort to patrol routes that avoid avalanche hazards. However, when evaluating an avalanche hazard, there is often a high degree of uncertainty. When mistakes are made, the consequences are high. Avalanches produce incredible energy. Soldiers caught in an avalanche may be injured or killed by blunt force trauma from collisions with rock, ice, and trees. Without an air pocket, unconsciousness may come in minutes, followed rapidly by permeant brain injury and death. Chapter 6 Mountain Mobility A unit's ability to maneuver through difficult and hazardous terrain provides it with access to the most tactically advantageous areas in the mountains. Units with Soldiers trained to a high level of mobility can move further, faster, and more safely through all levels of terrain. Mobility skill is the primary tool to manage risk when there is a fall hazard. Rope systems and belays can be used to mitigate fall risk during movement but require more time to complete, more technical training to accomplish, and can result in increased exposure to enemy attack. By far, the greatest combat multiplier in the mountains is high mobility skill. Units anticipating combat operations should focus on building individual movement skills over nearly all other special technical or tactical skills. SECTION I - INDIVIDUAL MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES 6-1. Quality footwear, such as mountaineering boots, reduces many risks associated with moving in mountainous terrain. Quality boots increase both mobility and security of footing and can reduce orthopedic injuries. Boots designed for mountaineering range in weight, breathability, flexibility, and in how well they interface with other equipment. The rand helps protect the toe area from sharp rock and standing water. They have a high enough upper boot to protect the wearer's ankles from sharp rock and provide joint support against rolling. They have recessed soles made of softer rubber, a protective band around the forefoot, at least a partial shank, and are constructed with abrasion and water-resistant materials. Mountain Mobility 6-24. General techniques for ascending: * As terrain becomes steeper, routes should adopt a traversing or switchback pattern. This involves moving diagonally up and across a slope, then turning back and doing the same in the opposite direction as necessary. This switchback pattern reduces the intensity and demand on large muscle groups, slows the onset of fatigue, and allows Soldiers to maintain situational awareness. Charging in a straight line up a steep hill is more demanding, results in more extreme fatigue and longer recovery time, and increases the likelihood of slips, falls, and injury. This technique should be avoided unless speed is critical, and all members of the group are highly fit and experienced moving this way. * The rest step technique involves locking out the rear leg briefly with each step. This gives muscles a micro rest with each step and results in greater endurance over long movements. (See figure 6-2, page 88.) * Pressure breathing-this technique involves breathing all the way out on the exhale to empty the lungs of air. This does two positive things. involves breathing all the way out on the exhale to empty the lungs of air. This does two positive things. Chapter 6 SCRAMBLING 6-33. Scrambling is the act of moving over difficult or broken terrain, characterized by using mostly walking techniques but requires some use of the hands for balance or other specific climbing techniques. It is perhaps the most dangerous means of mobility in which snow and ice are not present. At the lowest level, scrambling involves simply placing a hand or hands on features periodically to help maintain balance and improve efficiency during movement. At the higher level, scrambling involves Soldiers making multiple easy rock-climbing moves, followed by several steps walking, and repeating that sequence throughout an ascent. 6-34. Typically, 3rd-class terrain is where Soldiers begin scrambling, but just exactly what terrain and terrain features require is determined largely by the mobility skill of the individual Soldier. Soldiers with low-mobility skill will need to use hands more often, especially if a fall risk is present, which will slow their movement. Soldiers with higher mobility skills need to use their hands less often for balance enabling them to move faster even when a fall risk is present. 6-35. They are finding and selecting suitable holds and positioning the body to achieve sufficient friction for continued movement. Due to the vertical nature of the terrain, hands must be used to aid Soldiers in maintaining balance and preventing them from tipping backward off the rock. 6-52. Suspect rock-climbing holds should be tested to ensure they are secure by tapping with a hand or foot. Holds that move or shift should be avoided. This is common in undeveloped 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Maintaining Balance 6-53. Balance is the most important aspect of rock climbing and footwork is the foundation of balance. Good use of the feet saves energy and makes staying in balance easier. A relaxed, comfortable

undeveloped 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Maintaining Balance 6-53. Balance is the most important aspect of rock climbing and footwork is the foundation of balance. Good use of the feet saves energy and makes staying in balance easier. A relaxed, comfortable stance is essential. The body should be centered over the feet as much as possible. On lower angle sections of climbing, it should be positioned away from the rock face. Alternatively, it should be positioned closer to the rock face on steeper sections. This puts downward pressure on footholds, increasing their security. Smaller lower body movements are often less strenuous than larger ones, which take more effort to stay in balance. 6-54. Rock climbing usually requires the use of handholds to maintain balance. Handholds can be large jugs that allow climbers to hold nearly their whole weight or tiny crimpers that only hold a fraction of their weight. Specific handhold techniques are discussed throughout this section. New climbers commonly overuse their arms to pull themselves up the rock and burn out quickly. Tired or pumped forearms are a sign of bad footwork. 6-55. Whenever possible, three points of contact should be maintained while moving the fourth to the next hold.

The body is then positioned away from the rock so that the foot does not slip. The

Chapter 6 Figure 6-14. Liebacking Crack Climbing 6-68. Crack climbing requires a specific set of nonintuitive techniques that take quite a bit of practice to build proficiency in. While some climbs involving cracks can be climbed with weak or no crack technique, more difficult crack climbs require climbing shoes and good technique to be climbable. Mixed crack climbing involves using features on the rock face for footholds while using a prominent crack for handholds. (See figure 6-15.) Classic crack climbing involves moving up a prominent crack by alternately jamming hands or fingers and feet or toes and walking them up the crack. Often, one foot is placed out of the crack to the side for balance, even on a featureless face. Off-width crack climbing is the term for climbing cracks that are larger than fist and foot sized but not large enough to fit the entire body. Mountain Mobility Figure 6-15. Mixed face and crack climbing Jamming 6-69. A critical technique in climbing cracks involves placing a hand or foot into a crack and turning, twisting, or otherwise manipulating them so that they become temporarily jammed in the crack. A good jam can be achieved in a variety of ways depending on crack size, whether it has constrictions in it or not, and its position in relation to other holds on the climb. Jams can provide solid hands or footholds but are often uncomfortable or even painful. Crack size determines which jam technique to use for a given hold. Constrictions in the crack make jam holds more secure. Types of Hand Jams 6-70. Hand-sized jams are the easiest to perform. The hand is inserted open into the crack and then the fingers bent exert pressure against the walls of the crack. Often turning one hand thumb down is useful. Typically, leaning to the same side adds security to a thumb up hand jam. (See figure 6-16, page 104 for variations of hand jamming.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 103

The same jamming principles apply, but climbers just insert their entire fist into the crack. (See figure 6-17 for variations of fist jamming.) 6-72. Finger jams are techniques necessary for cracks that are smaller than those that will accept a hand. The same jamming principles apply, but the climber only inserts their fingers, or parts of their fingers into the crack. Finger jamming is more difficult and can be painful for the joints. It is important to strengthen finger muscles prior to attempting to support substantial weight with finger jams to prevent joint strain. (See figure 6-18.) Types of Foot Jams 6-73. Foot jams involve turning the foot so that it fits into the crack and then twisting it so that the width of the foot wedges into the crack. This can be uncomfortable but can provide very secure footholds. (See figure 6-19.) 6-74. Toe jams are used in the same manner as foot jams, but in smaller cracks. (See figure 6-20, page 106.) Chapter 6 Figure 6-20. Toe jams Figure 6-21. Arm bar and chicken wing Dihedral and Chimney Climbing 6-77. Climbing dihedrals and chimneys involves positioning the body inside a feature and using counterpressure or stemming to make upward movement. These features can often make for less strenuous climbing due to the counterpressure positions allowing for more rests. A dihedral is two rock faces that meet to form a corner, like an open book. Often there is a crack where the two faces meet. Chimneys are roughly parallel-sided features. They could be like a vertical shaft or crack large enough to accept a whole body. 6-78. Dihedrals can usually be climbed with a combination of stemming and either crack or face climbing. Dihedrals are easier and less strenuous to climb when the two faces have multiple and large features. 6-79. Chimneys are often unpleasant features to climb but provide a lot of security during movement. The basic technique for climbers is to position their body in the chimney and use counterpressure by pushing with arms, legs, and back against opposing sides. Climbers lean heavily in the direction they want to move and place hands on available holds, and then walk their feet in the same direction using available footholds. Sometimes a crossover step is helpful. This technique typically requires solid side pulling, counterpressure, and counterforce skills. (See figure 6-26.) Figure 6-25. Often low holds located near where climbers want to put their feet need to be used to get over the edge. Often, a mantling technique is effective. Most importantly, climbers should avoid laying on their belly on the edge when moving because it may be difficult to get their feel back on the rock, and they may slide off on sloped ledges. Beginner rock-climbing training is typically conducted at established climbing areas using top rope belay techniques (see chapter 10). When supervised by qualified mountaineers, this kind of rock climbing is relatively low risk and has a high payoff for developing mobility skills. One restriction is that sites do not often allow large groups to be actively engaged. Thus, climbing training should be planned along with concurrent training for smaller groups to rotate through. Route difficulty should be challenging to climbers but easy enough that they can be successful. This motivates climbers to build skills. A motivational rather than critical atmosphere is most effective when building climbing skills. 6-90. Climbing training for more advanced military mountaineers can be conducted the same way, just on more challenging routes, but should also be conducted in a multipitch setting that more accurately reproduces conditions of climbing during military operations. This setting requires the development of lead climbing and route-finding skills, which are critical to the advanced military mountaineer. 6-91. Leaders should try to learn the etiquette associated with climbing before using civilian climbing areas. 112 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility SECTION II - MOVEMENT OVER SNOW AND ICE 6-92. Deep snow, steep powdery slopes, glare ice, and frozen waterfalls all present significant challenges to movement. The basic individual movement principles and skill development necessary for movement under other surface conditions also apply to movement over snow and ice. However, additional skills are necessary for efficiency and safety. Specialized equipment is required in even the easiest snow or ice-covered terrain. MOBILITY OVER SNOW AND ICE 6-93. Fitness and movement techniques are the foundation of moving through snow or up steep ice. However, identifying and selecting secure foot placements can be difficult because traction is drastically reduced. Movement without specialized equipment, such as crampons or skis, is difficult under almost all conditions above 1st-class terrain. Even when it is possible, deep snow requires a substantial amount of energy to move through unaided. Anything deeper than calf-deep snow will impede movement in even easy terrain, and a few inches of snow or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills

or a glaze of ice will make steeper terrain treacherous. Soldiers must develop the same level of skill using snow and ice equipment, which requires proficiency in an additional set of skills. Like moving over broken rocky terrain, these skills can only be developed through experience and repetition. Units that train their Soldiers to proficiency in these conditions can move faster, safer, and access terrain that others cannot. EQUIPMENT FOR SNOW AND ICE 6-94. Skis provide substantial floatation in deep snow and require the least amount of energy for movement. This is especially true for downhill movement where much energy can be saved over walking. There are varieties of ski systems available for movement over snow, but those most suited to military mountaineering are called alpine touring skis. The ski itself is like a downhill ski, but the binding allows the heel to release for movement over flat or uphill terrain. It can also be locked down for greater control when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is

when skiing downhill. Climbing skins are used in conjunction with skis to climb uphill. Skins are designed to slide in only one direction, providing traction in deep snow and on steep slopes. At a minimum, a stiff mountaineering boot is necessary for use with skis. In the steepest terrain, a dedicated rigid plastic ski boot may be required. Compatibility between boots and bindings must be considered. (See figure 6-28, page 114.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 113

Chapter 6 Figure 6-28. Alpine touring skis 6-95. Snowshoes are another tool available to Soldiers for moving over deep snow. Snowshoes work with any boot. (See figure 6-29.) 114 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Sleds are useful for carrying large amounts of equipment, such as bivouac equipment, heavy weapons, food and water, or other supplies. They range in size, shape, and weight, all of which should be considered before selection for military operations. Four- and ten-Soldier Ahkio-style sleds are available through the military supply system. Chapter 6 Figure 6-30. Ahkio sleds 6-98. Crampons attach to the Soldier's boot to provide traction on ice and snow. There are two basic types: general mountaineering crampons and ice climbing crampons. Mountaineering crampons have less aggressive points. They are designed for use in steep snow and on low-angle ice and can be used for ice climbing but are not ideal. Ice climbing crampons have points that are more aggressive and are typically more rigid. They are designed for steep ice climbing but can be used in snow and low angle ice as well. Crampons work best when paired with a stiff leather or rigid plastic mountaineering boot. They do not work well with issued cold-weather combat boots. (See figure 6-31.) Figure 6-31. Crampons 6-99. Mountain axes are important tools for movement over steep snow and occasional low-angle ice. The two types of axes usually used in alpine terrain are general mountain axes and hybrid mountain axes. Chapter 6 Figure 6-33. Ice tools MILITARY OPERATIONS IN SNOW- AND ICE-COVERED TERRAIN 6-101. Snow and ice present many additional challenges for units that need to move in mountainous terrain. Specialized equipment, training, and experience are necessary to move in it safely and effectively. Whether the challenges are deep snow, slick slopes, or steep sections of vertical ice, they will prove substantial obstacles for unprepared units. Units anticipating operating in such terrain and conditions should train in them prior to engaging in combat operations. 6-102. Even with proper equipment and training, it is unlikely that larger units can move in terrain steeper than 2nd-class terrain without ropes due to the high risk of long sliding falls. Small teams of advanced military mountaineers should be trained to move over ice and snow and tasked with finding routes and establishing rope systems for larger units. Mountain Mobility MOVEMENT OVER SNOW 6-103. Low- to moderate-angle snow slopes found on or adjacent to valleys are primary avenues of movement for military units operating in winter conditions. Steeper slopes in gullies and passes are often the easiest routes through even steeper rocky features around them. Though challenging to move over, these often provide the best access to points of domination in alpine terrain. 6-104. Chapter 6 Figure 6-34. Step cutting GLISSADING 6-108. Glissading is a technique used to descend low to moderate angle slopes by sliding in the seated position and using a mountain axe as a brake. (See figure 6-35.) Glissading allows Soldiers to descend appropriate slopes very quickly and efficiently, thereby saving significant time and energy. Specific conditions are required for glissading to be appropriate. The slope should not have any obstacles (such as trees, rocks, drop offs, crevasses) in the slide path, and it should have sufficient soft snow on the surface to allow Soldiers to control the speed of the slide. Glissading should never be done on hard-packed snow or ice surfaces. Crampons should be removed prior to glissading to ensure injuries to lower extremities are not caused by a crampon becoming caught on something during the slide. 6-109. Glissading is conducted by sitting in the snow and positioning the midpoint of a mountain axe shaft against one hip with the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain

the spike in the snow. The hand on the same side as the axe holds its shaft to the hip at the midpoint. The other hand holds the top of the axe where pick, shaft and adze meet. The mountain axe pick should always face forward (away from the Soldier) to prevent injury. Soldiers then initiate the slide on their buttocks using the axe spike as a brake. To slow down, Soldiers rotate the spike downward, pressing it deeper into the snowpack and increasing friction. To speed up, Soldiers rotate the spike away from the snowpack, decreasing friction. Adequate time should be allowed between Soldiers sliding in the same glissade path to ensure a collision does not occur should a Soldier stop shortly mid-slide. 120 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-35. Glissading FLATFOOTING 6-110. Flatfooting is the term for numerous techniques that increase security and efficiency of movement over snow and ice slopes. These techniques involve the use of both crampons and a mountain axe. The key principle of flatfooting is to position the body so that all crampon points are embedded in the snow surface. This provides maximum security for foot placements. These techniques are particularly critical to safe movement over steep, hard-packed snow. Flatfooting with heavy loads requires greater proficiency. Flatfooting techniques are much more difficult to perform in flexible boots or with loose sloppy crampons. (See figure 6-36, page 122.) 6-111. Crampons substantially increase the security of foot placements when used properly. However, walking in them forces the Soldier's gait to change and can take some practice getting used to. They must be sized properly and snugged tight to the boot, so Soldiers' boots do not slide around in the crampon introducing instability to their foot placements. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 121

Footwork techniques used in rock climbing, such as edging, are very insecure when wearing crampons. They should not be used. Ankles must be rolled somewhat downhill to ensure crampon points are embedded in the surface. Mountain Mobility 6-114. To obtain secure foot placements, lean the body away from the slope to increase pressure on crampon points. This becomes more important as surface conditions get firmer. Generally, it is easier to stay in balance and achieve solid foot placements by taking smaller steps. Moving diagonally up slope makes this easier to execute. 6-115. Flatfooting, using a mountain axe in a cross-body position. To perform this technique, the Soldier stands sideways to the slope. The mountain axe head is held in the downhill hand and the shaft held low in the uphill hand. The uphill foot is placed perpendicular to the slope and the downhill foot is placed similarly, but with the toe pointed downhill as much as comfort demands. The axe spike is then forced into the snowpack uphill from the feet far enough so that most of the Soldier's weight is transitioned onto it. This provides balance and security during foot movement. The downhill foot is moved across and placed above the uphill foot. If the crossover step is too awkward, it can be moved to a position just below the uphill foot, but this method is less efficient. The Soldier's weight is then transitioned

Chapter 6 6-117. Front pointing involves kicking into the slope with the toe of the boot so that all front crampon points become embedded in the surface. The Soldier leans forward slightly locking the ankle so that the sole of the foot is held perpendicular to the slope. If the heel is too low or too high, or only the large front points are embedded, then the foot placement will be less secure and may fail. The Soldier stands up on the placement using hands or mountain axe for balance and repeats kicking in with the other foot higher on the slope. This process is repeated as the Soldier generally moves straight up the slope. The front-pointing technique is very effective and allows for faster movement in steep terrain but is more physically taxing. The Soldier's calf muscles become fatigued quickly using this technique. The front-pointing technique is most effective for ascending short, steep sections of terrain. (See figure 6-40.) Figure 6-40. Front pointing 6-118. Chapter 6 Figure 6-44. Descending steep slopes SELF-ARREST 6-127. Self-arrest is a technique intended to stop a short fall before it turns into a long, sliding, tumbling fall. Soldiers that will be moving on moderate to steep snow slopes unroped must be issued a mountain axe at a minimum and trained to proficiency in self-arrest techniques. There is little margin for error in executing self-arrest on steep slopes with firm surface conditions. Self-arresting should not be considered an adequate protective measure when slipping and falling risk is determined to be likely. Good movement skills are still the primary risk mitigation for moving unroped. 6-128. Soldiers should carry the axe in the cane position with the pick to the rear in the uphill hand. The instant Soldiers fall, they must commit to self-arresting immediately. The technique is executed by bringing the mountain axe into position at the center of chest, with the hand on its head and pick facing away. The lower hand moves to a position low on the axe shaft. The Soldier then uses body weight and violence of action to drive the pick into the snowpack. This must be done in seconds and if the axe is not

lower hand moves to a position low on the axe shaft. The Soldier then uses body weight and violence of action to drive the pick into the snowpack. This must be done in seconds and if the axe is not centered under the body, it is difficult to apply adequate force to achieve this. The less aggressive and curved design of the ice axe pick is meant to prevent it from biting into the surface too well, where momentum would cause it to be ripped out of the falling Soldiers' hands. Rather, it is designed to stop the Soldier gradually. For this reason, picks that are more aggressive like those found on tools meant for ice climbing are less effective for this. If crampons are not worn, the Soldier can also dig toes into the snowpack to assist stopping the slide. Careful attention must be paid not to allow the spike of the axe to dig into the snow while sliding. If this happens, the Soldier could be flipped over backwards and thrown into a tumble. Recovering from a tumbling is unlikely. (See figure 6-45.) 6-129. When self-arresting with crampons on, Soldiers must bend their knees during the slide, so

sliding. If this happens, the Soldier could be flipped over backwards and thrown into a tumble. Recovering from a tumbling is unlikely. (See figure 6-45.) 6-129. When self-arresting with crampons on, Soldiers must bend their knees during the slide, so the crampon points do not catch and cause a tumble. Legs must remain bent until sliding has stopped. Front points can then be planted to reduce the likelihood of a slide resuming. 6-130. To self-arrest while sliding on the back, the Soldier must bring the axe into position at the center of the chest, then roll in the direction of the axe head until on the stomach, and then drive the pick into the snow. 6-131. To self-arrest headfirst face down, the Soldier must reach downhill to the same side as the axe head, plant the pick, pivot the body around the pick, and swing the legs downhill. 6-132. Self-arrest headfirst, on the back, is the most difficult. Here, the Soldier must plant the pick, twist and roll toward the pick, swing the legs downhill, and roll the chest toward the pick. 128 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Mountain Mobility Figure 6-47. Alpine ice 6-137. All the hazards associated with rock climbing exist for ice climbing, as well as additional ones, including avalanches and icefalls. Icefall is always a real threat to ice climbers and personnel located below them. This is particularly true during warmer temperatures as hanging ice features can break off and fall naturally. Ice climbers are at higher risk of injury during a fall due to the sharp tools and crampons used in climbing. Chapter 7 Navigation in Mountainous Terrain The goals, strategies, and tools available to Soldiers for navigation in mountainous terrain are no different from other types of terrain. However, mountainous terrain makes using those tools to stay on course much more difficult. Additionally, straying off course while navigating in this terrain can prove extremely hazardous and detrimental to mission success. The difficulty of planning routes and calculating movement timelines also increases significantly with the steepness and complexity of terrain. Soldiers and leaders who learn how to mitigate these challenges effectively can not only successfully navigate in mountainous terrain but also better use the terrain for cover and concealment. SECTION I - MILITARY LAND NAVIGATION IN NONTECHNICAL MOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN 7-1. Navigation is the process of determining one's present position, locating a target objective, and selecting and following a route between these two points. Navigation consists of three distinct stages: orientation, navigation, and route finding. 7-2. Orientation is simply figuring out exactly where one is. Using a map, compass, and identifiable terrain features, assisted by an altimeter and GPS, is the foundation of good orientation. 7-3. Navigation determines the objective's location and the direction from the Soldier's starting point to the objective. The

one is. Using a map, compass, and identifiable terrain features, assisted by an altimeter and GPS, is the foundation of good orientation. 7-3. Navigation determines the objective's location and the direction from the Soldier's starting point to the objective. The same skills and equipment used in orientation are essential for good navigation. 7-4. Route finding is picking the best line of travel IAW METT-TC (I); mission, enemy, terrain and weather, troops and support available, time available, civil considerations, and informational considerations, and the commander's intent. Good route finding in mountainous terrain requires solid terrain analysis, clear priorities for route selection, an understanding of group members' levels of fitness and mobility skill, unit capabilities for technical movement, and mission-specific requirements. Examples of priorities for route selection are navigability of terrain, tactical advantage and disadvantage throughout the movement, concealment throughout, fatigue reduction, and required speed of movement. 7-5. Perhaps the single, most important factor in navigation through mountainous terrain is the ability to identify and analyze terrain. to identify and analyze terrain. Navigators must be able to create an accurate mental model of the terrain to be moved through from a map or satellite imagery. The more skilled they are at this, the more effective they will be at avoiding hazards, selecting tactically advantageous or concealed routes, and planning paths that minimize fatigue. This ability can only be developed effectively through route planning and movement in such terrain. When climbing, rappelling, or building rope installations, the mountaineer must know how to utilize and maintain this equipment. Misuse can cause serious injury or death. This chapter discusses equipment, terminology, knots, hitches, rope management techniques, care, and maintenance. SECTION I - TYPES OF ROPE, WEBBING, AND CARABINERS 8-1. Mountaineering equipment is engineered to be lightweight but strong enough to provide a wide margin of safety. Each item is tested to high standards. In most cases, user error is to blame when this equipment fails. Soldiers should regularly check and inspect mountaineering equipment. Equipment should be replaced when there is any obvious damage, or it has exceeded the manufacturer's lifecycle recommendation. 8-2. All mountaineering equipment used in training should be constructed and tested to a recognized standard. Military mountaineers need to be able to differentiate between the two and know how each rope should be used. STATIC ROPE 8-5. A static rope is a kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling, lowering, and anchor systems construction. It has a core (kern) that is laid straight, giving it low stretch (2 to 8 percent). They are constructed with a tightly woven sheath (mantle) and are more durable than dynamic ropes. Static ropes are preferred for rappelling, rescue operations, load hauling, and rope installations. They should never be used in situations where the rope is shock loaded (for example, lead climbing). Typical diameter for static rope is between 9 and 11 millimeters (mm). Static rope is issued in 600 feet (183 meters) spools. While the minimum tensile strength for static ropes for military use is 4,500 pounds, the recommended working load is often 25 percent of the actual strength of that rope. Oval carabiners were once popular for general mountaineering because their symmetry makes them good for many purposes. Most carabiners used today are offset D-shaped carabiners, which offer the best compromise of weight to strength and ease of clipping and racking. (See figure 8-4.) 152 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Knot Tying and Rope Management Figure 8-4. Carabiner components 8-15. A carabiner's design allows it to be loaded in opposite directions along the spine. (See figure 8-4.) When loaded improperly, the strength of a carabiner is reduced significantly. When using a carabiner, care should be taken to avoid cross loading the carabiner across the gate and spine and to avoid tri-loading. (See figure 8-5, page 154.) 8-16. There are two types of carabiners used in mountaineering: the locking carabiner and the nonlocking carabiner. LOCKING CARABINERS 8-17. Locking carabiners feature a barrel-shaped sleeve that prevents the gate from opening. They are used where an accidental carabiner opening could cause system failure. Any live load should be attached to an anchor with a locking carabiner. Locking carabiners are used for rappel hook ups, personal safeties, and the primary attachments in most rope systems. (See figure 8-5, page 154.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 153

Chapter 8 Figure 8-5. Improper carabiner loading NONLOCKING CARABINERS 8-18. Most carabiners do not lock. Locking mechanisms add weight and slow the manipulation of carabiners. Nonlocking carabiners are used in most mountaineering applications. They should be used where there is more than one attachment and accidental gate opening will not cause system failure. SECTION II - BASIC TERMINOLOGY 8-19. Understanding basic terminology is important when learning how to tie knots. The terms explained in this section are the most common in military mountaineering. (See figure 8-6, page 156.) RUNNING END 8-20. A running end is the loose or working end of the rope. STANDING END 8-21. The standing end is the static, stationary, or nonworking end of the rope. 154 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Knot Tying and Rope Management BIGHT 8-22. A bight of rope is a bend in the rope in which the standing end is parallel to the running end and the rope does not cross itself. LOOP 8-23. A loop is a bend of the rope in which the rope crosses itself. When the running end crosses over the top of the standing end, it is an overhand loop. When the running end crosses under the standing end, it is an underhand loop. TURN 8-24. A turn wraps around an object, providing 360° contact. ROUND TURN 8-25. A round turn wraps around an object one and one-half times so that the running and standing end are parallel. A round turn is used to hold an anchor or knot in place. HALF HITCH 8-26. A half hitch is a turn with the running end crossing over the standing end. TAIL 8-27. The tail is the excess portion of the running end of the rope when the knot is completed. If a knot requires an overhand safety, the length of the tail is measured from the safety knot to the end of the rope. A safety knot is a backup knot tied to

the rope when the knot is completed. If a knot requires an overhand safety, the length of the tail is measured from the safety knot to the end of the rope. A safety knot is a backup knot tied to prevent a primary knot from slipping loose. DRESSING 8-28. Dressing a knot is arranging all the knot parts, removing unnecessary kinks, twists, and slack so that all rope parts of the knot are secured and tight. SETTING 8-29. Setting a knot is removing all unnecessary slack from the knot. This ensures that the knot is tight and minimizes the chances of the knot becoming untied. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 155

Chapter 8 Figure 8-6. Examples of rope-tying terminology SECTION III - KNOT TYING AND CONSIDERATIONS 8-30. The term knot is commonly used to describe numerous categories. A knot is the fixed portion of a rope that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the process of being tied for some purpose. Sometimes it is referred to as a "hard knot" since its condition will remain intact until actively untied. Knots are self-contained and self-supporting and do not need another object or rope to maintain its integrity. Hitches are not considered knots. Yet, for simplicity, they are generalized into a single category. Knots should never be considered permanent. It is possible that they can loosen or become less secure under certain conditions. Knots should be inspected regularly. Many knots can accomplish the same task; therefore, it is important to understand these considerations when choosing the appropriate knot to tie. TYPES OF KNOTS 8-31. There are several broad types of knots that are used in mountaineering. Military mountaineers should be familiar with the following types and terms at a minimum. BENDS 8-32. Bends are used to join the ends of rope, cord, or webbing. When tied correctly, they are

of knots that are used in mountaineering. Military mountaineers should be familiar with the following types and terms at a minimum. BENDS 8-32. Bends are used to join the ends of rope, cord, or webbing. When tied correctly, they are considered safe and strong enough for many applications. Specific joining knots should be used for certain situations and applications. Take care to learn the purpose of each joining knot and to have a clear understanding of where, when, and why to use each one. HITCHES 8-33. Hitches are like knots but are tied around another object or rope. Without an object like a carabiner or another rope, a hitch would not retain its form and fall apart. 156 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Knot Tying and Rope Management FRICTION HITCHES 8-34. A friction hitch is a type of hitch tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily while no force is applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned. Friction hitches grip the rope while under load, but they can be moved along the rope when unloaded. There are several friction hitches, each with different applications. Using the wrong friction hitch can be dangerous or create additional problems. LOOP KNOTS 8-35. Loop knots are used to create fixed or adjustable loops in rope or webbing. Some loops are directional to prevent the distortion of a knot when loaded. SPECIALTY KNOTS 8-36. These knots do not fit the above criteria but are still useful to know. They may only serve one specific purpose for mountaineering. KNOT TYING CONSIDERATIONS 8-37. There are several factors to consider when selecting knots for use or training. Military mountaineers do not need to be able to tie every possible knot that can be used in mountaineering. They just need to be able to tie an appropriate knot for each application they may face in their duties. When selecting knots for use in

to be able to tie every possible knot that can be used in mountaineering. They just need to be able to tie an appropriate knot for each application they may face in their duties. When selecting knots for use in mountaineering rigging, selecting simpler knots that are easier to tie, untie, and inspect are preferable to complex specialty knots, even if the complex knot is a little more effective. When considering teaching knot tying techniques to Soldiers and new military mountaineers, knots that are easier to teach and learn are preferred, as are multipurpose knots. Ultimately, the number and complexity of knots that military mountaineers may need to be proficient with increases as the scope and complexity of their technical mountaineering responsibilities and duties increase. It is important to prepare all ropes before departing on a mission. Avoid rope preparation in the field. PACKAGING 8-129. New ropes should be carefully unspooled or uncoiled to avoid kinks and prevent tangling. Coil 8-130. A coil is a secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling. The ends must be heated to the melting point to attach the inner core strands to the outer sheath. By fusing the two together, the sheath cannot slide backward or forward. when handling ropes: * While in use, do not allow the rope to touch sharp edges. Rope is cut more easily when under tension. If the rope must be used over a sharp edge, pad the edge for protection and inspect often. * Never allow one rope to continuously run over another. any faucet. Pinholes within the pipe force water to circulate around and scrub the rope as the Soldier slowly feeds it through the washer. * Ropes should not be stored wet. Chapter 9 Anchor Selection and Construction Understanding anchors is an important fundamental that must be understood early in the path to becoming a military mountaineer. An anchor is the point where manufactured equipment for mountaineering meets the surface of the earth. Great varieties of natural features are found in different operational environments that a Soldier could use to construct an anchor. Anchors are found in all rope systems and are built in many ways. This chapter gives Soldiers the tools to assess terrain for the suitability of anchor construction for a wide variety of rope systems. This chapter also exposes Soldiers to the principles of anchor construction that ensure they are building solid anchors in a wide variety of terrain for many different purposes. Anchor selection in mountainous terrain requires a certain degree of knowledge and substantial experience. Most mountaineering accidents occur at the anchor. Inexperienced Soldiers should stick to selecting anchor features that are obviously stronger than necessary and choose simple rigging techniques with which they are familiar. An anchor for military mountaineering is a fixed object to which a rope system is secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. It is a point in the operational environment, which a rope installation is attached, providing more than enough resistance to a directional pull. Rope systems can be used for moving casualties and equipment. Some, like rappels or fixed ropes, are used for aiding movement. Technical rope systems provide the tools for addressing many of the challenges posed by mountainous terrain. Anchor selection and evaluation together form the foundation of all systems. 9-2. Considerations for selecting a natural feature to construct an anchor are its location and ability to resist any forces that are placed upon it. The anchor should be above any intended rope pathways. This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform

This reduces the pendulum effect on any loads attached to the anchor. Another important facet of anchor location is its proximity to the edge. In some situations, having the anchor a short distance away from the edge creates a platform to work on. In other situations, such as setting a top rope, it is best to have the anchor near the edge. This aspect of anchor building can be challenging as the strength of natural features, such as rocks, trees, roots, and boulders; can be difficult to judge. Soldiers must err on the side of caution and leave no doubt that an anchor is strong enough for its intended purpose. If there is any doubt about a single-point anchor's strength or security, then additional anchor components should be constructed and incorporated until sufficient strength and security are achieved to ensure that anchor failure cannot occur. The strength of an anchor should never be in question. 9-3. Anchors in mountaineering should be loaded in a steady and slow manner. Avoid bouncing as much as possible as it could weaken the integrity of the natural object being used. Sometimes slack can generate in various types of rope systems and cause an anchor

Chapter 9 SECTION II - TREES 9-18. Tree anchors should be considered for use first. They are usually strong and often simple to construct with minimal use of equipment. Trees are already in place and simply require a method of attaching the rope. However, they should be carefully studied and evaluated for stability and strength before use. Sometimes the rope is tied directly to the anchor, but under most circumstances, a cord or sling is attached to the tree and then the climbing rope is attached to the sling with a carabiner. CONSIDERATIONS 9-19. The following are considerations for using trees as anchors for mountaineering rope systems: * In rocky terrain, trees usually have a shallow root system. This can be evaluated by pushing on the tree to see how well it is rooted. If there is concern that a tree may be pulled over when loaded, another anchor should be selected. rope should be anchored as low as possible to reduce leverage. * When evaluating a tree for suitable strength, strive for a diameter at the base of the tree of at least 8 inches. * In the summer months, it may be easy to determine if a tree is alive. The best indicator can be leaves. However, even trees that have fallen over may still grow leaves if they are still partially rooted. Ensure that a concentrated effort is made to evaluate the tree. * In the winter, certain trees do not have leaves. This may make it difficult to establish if they are alive. A high-strength tie off is a single-point anchoring method that retains maximum installation rope strength and releasability, using multiple-round turns around the anchor object to create friction, and securing the end back to itself ensuring no force is applied to any component knots or carabiners. It is used to anchor the rope on high-load installations used for bridging and traversing. (See figure 9-9, page 206.) The wraps of the rope around the anchor absorb the tension of the installation and keep the tension off the knot and carabiner. The anchor is usually tied with a minimum of three wraps, more, if necessary, to absorb the tension. A smooth anchor may require several wraps, whereas a rough barked tree might only require a few. The rope is wrapped from top to bottom without crossing strands so that it can be untied under tension, if desired. A fixed loop is placed into the end of the rope and attached loosely back onto the rope with a locking carabiner. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 205

Chapter 9 Figure 9-11. Chockstone used in a construction TUNNELS, ARCHES, AND PINCH POINTS 9-26. Tunnels and arches are holes formed in solid rock. If viable, they provide one of the more secure natural anchor points as they can be pulled in any direction (See figure 9-12.) A natural anchor is a natural fixed object (such as a tree, rock formation, or ice formation) to which a rope system can be secured and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. A pinch-point anchor is used the same way as arches or tunnels; it is just formed by a pinch point between two large boulders, allowing a sling or cordelette to be tied around it. Artificial rock protection is anything used to protect a climber or anchor a rope system and is not part of the natural environment. The evolution of artificial protection started with handmade pieces of metal called pitons. Now there are several companies that manufacture various lightweight artificial protection. Chapter 9 and can be difficult to remove. Removable protection refers to spring-loaded camming devices (known as cams), chocks, and other specialty protection that is easily recoverable after use. 9-28. Artificial protection is used to construct anchors in various ways. Anchors may be comprised of a combination of artificial protection and other objects, such as a tree or a boulder. The combinations are endless. However, when building anchors made with only artificial protection, multiple pieces are required. No single piece of artificial protection is considered adequate to comprise an anchor. A minimum of two components are needed to provide redundancy in the case of bad placement, poor rock quality, or any other factor causing a piece to fail. PITONS 9-29. Pitons have been in use for over 100 years. Although still available, pitons are not used as often as other types of artificial anchors due primarily to their impact on the environment. Most climbers prefer to use other artificial anchors rather than pitons because they do not scar the rock and are easier to remove. Pitons still have a place in military mountaineering since they are a relatively light, cheap, and expendable yet extremely strong and secure anchor option when

rather than pitons because they do not scar the rock and are easier to remove. Pitons still have a place in military mountaineering since they are a relatively light, cheap, and expendable yet extremely strong and secure anchor option when placed properly. They are particularly useful during rocky alpine descents, when an ice axe with a hammer is already carried and natural rappel anchors are scarce. 9-30. One piton is not considered strong or secure enough to serve as a single belay or system anchor. When establishing an anchor using multiple pitons, they should be placed in different cracks or features. A single piton can also be combined with other viable natural anchoring methods, if available. Note. Properly placing pitons requires significant practice to master, which should be conducted in training scenarios involving backup systems to protect the trainee should a placement fail. ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES 9-31. Some advantages with using pitons are- * Depending on type and placement, pitons can support multiple directions of pull. * They are less complex than other types of artificial anchors. * Pitons work well in thin cracks where other types of artificial anchors do not. 9-32. Anchor Selection and Construction INSTALLATION AND USE 9-44. There are enough differences in bolts available on the market that mountaineers should refer to manufacturers' instructions for installing bolts. Installing bolts permanently alters the rock. The climbing community has strong ethics regarding the placement of bolts. Ethics and regulations vary regionally, but in all areas, it is unacceptable to add bolts to existing climbs. Any bolting should be done with the consensus of the climbing community. 9-45. When using existing bolts as climbing protection or as part of an anchor system, mountaineers should inspect them for anything indicating compromise. The first thing that should be inspected is the rock on which it will be placed. Bolts are only as strong and secure as the quality of the rock. The hanger should not be rusty or loose. Loose hangers can indicate the bolt being insecure, or the hole has not been drilled deep enough to secure the hanger to the rock's face. If the nut holding a hanger can be tightened to a point, then it is viable. If it keeps spinning, the bolt should not be used or at the very least backed up with additional protection. 9-46. Using chocks in anchor construction has the following advantages: * Tactically quiet installation and recovery. * Usually easy to retrieve and, unless severely damaged, are reusable. * Light to carry. * Minimal rock scarring as opposed to pitons. * Sometimes can be placed where pitons cannot (expanding rock flakes where pitons would further weaken the rock). 9-49. Using chock in anchor construction has the following disadvantages: * May not fit in thin cracks, which may accept pitons. * Often provide only one direction of pull. * Practice and experience are necessary to become proficient in proper placement and removal. PLACEMENT 9-50. The principles of placing chocks are to find a crack with a constriction at some point, place a chock of appropriate size above and behind the constriction, and set the chock by gently jerking down. Maximum surface contact with a tight fit is critical. Chocks are usually good for a single direction of pull. 9-51. Avoid cracks that have crumbly (soft) or deteriorating rock, if possible. Some cracks may have loose rock, grass, and dirt, which should be removed before placing the chock. Look for a constriction point in the

single direction of pull. 9-51. Avoid cracks that have crumbly (soft) or deteriorating rock, if possible. Some cracks may have loose rock, grass, and dirt, which should be removed before placing the chock. Look for a constriction point in the crack, and then select a chock to fit it. 9-52. When selecting a chock, choose one that has as much surface area as possible in contact with the rock. A chock resting on one small crystal or point of rock is likely to be unsafe. A chock that sticks partly out of the crack is avoided. 9-53. All chocks used for lead climber protection should include a soft material extension, such as a runner, to prevent the rope from wiggling the chock out of placement. 218 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Anchor Selection and Construction 9-54. Chocks must be lightly tugged on to set them so that they do not fall out of placement. Weighting the placement helps to keep the protection in position. A carabiner often provides enough weight. CAMMING DEVICES 9-55. Camming devices are designed for building anchors in parallel-sided cracks where chocks are ineffective. There are several different types, but they all work by changing from a downward force to an outward force when loaded. This force creates enough friction that the device cannot move, even when no constriction in the crack is present. Camming devices increase force on surrounding rock as downward force is applied. Due to this, care should be taken to inspect the security of the rock on which they are placed. 9-56. Camming devices become even more secure when placed above a constriction. If the lobes slip during loading, they cannot exit the crack. 9-57. Cams are the most used camming devices in mountaineering. They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly. SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES 9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types

They have advantages and disadvantages and require extensive practice and experience to place and use properly. SPRING-LOADED CAMMING DEVICES 9-58. Cams are the most versatile and widely used artificial rock anchoring devices available to mountaineers. Although there are several types of cams, the modern design consists of two sets of lobes that oppose each other and rotate from one or two axles, connected to a trigger mechanism on a single, flexible stem that runs perpendicular to the axle. Attached to the axle is a presewn connection sling. They are designed to work in parallel-sided cracks where a chock would just slide down. 9-59. Cams come in a wide variety of sizes to fit cracks from 0.5 inches to over 21 inches. Each unit has an expansion range that enables it to function properly within a certain width of cracks. It may be necessary to carry many sizes depending upon the route, mission, and intended use. Most come with color-coded slings to help the user select the correct size for use. 9-60. Three quality camming devices equalized together are required to establish an adequate anchor. An exception is two large camming devices perfectly placed in solid rock with constrictions below them.

Chapter 10 Rope Systems for Climbing There is an inherent risk to moving in the mountains. Much of the terrain is high consequence, where a misjudged foothold, a loose rock, a slip, trip, or fall can kill. However, troops fighting in the mountains are often exposed to greater risk by not being able to move through the terrain. Examples exist throughout history. Modern examples include the assaults on Riva Ridge and Monte la Difensa in Italy, both examples of failed conventional assaults, where defensive positions in the heights were taken by assaults through more difficult terrain. More recently, the Indians retaking hilltops in the Kargil Conflict display all the same principles. Successful offensive operations in the mountains require troops who can move in difficult terrain and under poor conditions. The alternative is costly, often unsuccessful attacks where the defenders hold significant tactical advantage. To manage the risk involved with movement through these types of terrain, Soldiers must be trained in a variety of rope systems for climbing. SECTION I - RISK MITIGATION 10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one

a variety of rope systems for climbing. SECTION I - RISK MITIGATION 10-1. Fighting in the mountains requires exposure to mountain hazards. The mountain environment is defined by its hazards and difficulties. Often, the control measures used to address one hazard increase the exposure to another. Installing or using ropes to protect against a fall increases movement time and increases the exposure to compromise by enemy forces. MANAGING RISK 10-2. Managing risk in the mountains is a dynamic process, where the most appropriate measures for managing risk change with the terrain and situation. 10-3. Control measures target either the consequence or the likelihood of an incident. Protective equipment, such as a helmet to protect against rockfall, only reduces the consequence. The likelihood of being hit by rockfall is addressed by avoiding areas of loose rock and routing Soldiers so that they do not travel above one another. REDUCING THE LIKELIHOOD OF A FALL 10-4. The mountaineer has several technical tools for managing fall hazards. However, while the consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. Even a short fall while rock climbing can cause severe injury. To manage the risk, target factors that will reduce the likelihood

for managing fall hazards. However, while the consequence of a fall can be reduced, it cannot be eliminated. Even a short fall while rock climbing can cause severe injury. To manage the risk, target factors that will reduce the likelihood of a fall. JUDGEMENT 10-5. The safety of a mountaineer comes from the ability to read the terrain. Judge the rock, snow, or ice, and see where it can be climbed and where it cannot. This includes identifying features and weaknesses that can be linked together. Judgement is developed through time spent climbing in a controlled environment and through experience and mentorship. TECHNIQUE 10-6. Soldiers must possess the physical ability to make the moves, use footholds, and maintain balance as each move is made. As with judgement, climbing technique is the product of extensive training. LOAD 10-7. Increased Soldier load rapidly increases the difficulty of climbing, even in easy terrain. Operations in the mountains are subject to the mindset that occupying high terrain requires more equipment for sustaining life than at lower elevations. However, to maintain maneuverability, the Soldier's load must be reduced. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 235

Chapter 10 Soldiers conducting offensive operations, reconnaissance patrols, or any maneuver in high-consequence terrain need to travel light. FOOTWEAR 10-8. Proper footwear will enhance the military mountaineer's ability to move safely and efficiently through the rugged terrain found in the mountains. (See chapter 4 for footwear considerations.) ROPE 10-9. Ropes are used to reduce the consequence of a fall. Ropes can be fixed in place to manage or reduce the consequences of a fall (see chapter 11) or can be used to provide belays (see section III in this chapter). SECTION II - CONSIDERATIONS FOR MOVING UNROPED 10-10. Moving unroped is the fastest and most efficient method of moving through terrain. It requires little equipment and is quiet. Team members can move together, making communication quiet and easy. In instances where the greatest hazard is not falling, but rock or icefall, impending severe weather threat, enemy observation, or failing to meet an operational timeline, moving unroped may be the safest way to move. (See figure 10-1.) SECTION III - BELAYED CLIMBING 10-13. A belay is a system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier's fall should one occur. This section will discuss an overview of various strategies for using ropes and belays. TYPES OF BELAYED CLIMBING 10-14. When terrain is too dangerous to move unroped, a team will transition to belayed climbing. Belayed climbing is usually done in a party of two, with each climber tied into one end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other. TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. end of the rope. One team member is always anchored and providing a belay for the other. TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-15. Military mountaineers are first introduced to top rope climbing. Top rope climbing is where the rope is run through an anchor at the top of a climb and kept relatively snug to avoid longer falls. It is a training tool used to teach climbing technique. Chapter 10 LEAD CLIMBING 10-16. As military mountaineers progress, they are later introduced to lead climbing. Lead climbing is climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall protection with a belayer located below. When lead climbing, one climber leads climbs, placing protection and clipping the rope through it as they go. The belayer (sometimes referred to as the second) belays and is prepared to catch a fall. Lead climbers climb to another secure stance, build a solid anchor, and then belay second climbers as they climb to the new stance. Each length of climbing is called a pitch, which is a section of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a standard rope length (60 meters) on easy ice and snow. In more broken rock, it may be just 10 to 15 meters, to minimize rope drag and aid communication. 10-17. Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. Leaders accept more risk because they are climbing above their protection. Any fall will be well past the last piece of protection they placed before the rope begins

communication. 10-17. Lead climbing provides security for both members of the party. Leaders accept more risk because they are climbing above their protection. Any fall will be well past the last piece of protection they placed before the rope begins to come tight, so it is still imperative that leaders have good movement skills. The second has a top rope unless the route traverses. The overall security of the team is good. The team always has a solid attachment, and the belays can be placed in sheltered stances, with solid anchors. (See section V for more information on lead climbing.) 10-18. Most climbers will protect themselves with belays in 5th-class terrain. In 3rd- or 4th-class terrain, in darkness or bad weather, belayed climbing is the most conservative strategy for protecting the team and provides the greatest margin of safety. AID CLIMBING 10-19. If the climbing is too difficult for the leader, aid climbing is a climbing technique in which standing on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed protection is used to make upward progress.
