Simul-climbing is a belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while attached to the ends of a rope which runs through the fall protection. It is a variation of belayed climbing, where leaders continue to climb rather than stopping to belay the second. Second climbers climb simultaneously, removing protection as they go. Leaders continue to climb while trying to keep a few pieces of protection between the two climbers at all times. If one falls, they may pull their teammate off their stance, but they will be caught eventually, counterbalanced through the protection with the other climber. Simul-climbing is faster than belayed climbing and useful for covering easy ground quickly. (See figure 10-3, page 240.) Simul-climbing provides more security than soloing. Climbers may find it necessary to shorten ropes between 20 and 30 meters to help with communication and prevent rope drag. 10-22. When both climbers are moving together, both share the consequence of a fall. Climbers should only use simul-climbing where a fall is unlikely and with partners of similar ability. Rope Systems for Climbing Short Roping 10-24. Short roping is a technique that may have some use in training military mountaineers. (See figure 10-4, page 242.) Short roping is used by more experienced mountaineers for protecting less experienced Soldiers in easy but exposed terrain. The climbing rope is shortened to just a few meters, and the leader holds the rope close to the other's harness and the two move together. Short roping cannot arrest a fall. It manages risk by putting the senior mountaineer close to the other climber, where the senior mountaineer can coach and model. If someone slips, leaders pull the rope connected to their harness to prevent the slip from becoming a fall. The only anchor is the senior mountaineer's stance. Short roping is appropriate only in terrain where leaders are confident climbing unroped and do not need their hands to climb. 10-25. Short roping has limited application for military mountaineers. It is used when leaders need to use their hands to climb and cannot provide security with a short rope. Leaders place others in a safe position, and then scramble up the more technical section to a stance. From above, they can anchor or brace themselves to provide a belay as they climb. Often, because 4th-class terrain is more stepped, with plenty of ledges and stances, the leader can use simpler belay techniques and anchors than when rock climbing in 5th-class terrain and use a much shorter rope. 10-27. Most of the military mountaineer's time is spent avoiding the steepest and most difficult terrain. Operationally, they are more likely to use terrain where short pitching and simul-climbing would be most efficient. The techniques used in short pitching are faster than belayed climbing in longer pitches. A shorter rope helps with communication and fast transitions. 10-28. In a training environment, safety and conservative decision making must be the primary focus. As military mountaineers progress in their training, they may be exposed to alpine terrain above tree line. Weather and environmental hazards can pose a greater threat than falling. Each strategy for protecting the movement of the team is a compromise that should match the difficulty of terrain and the consequence of a fall. It should not expose the team to greater risk from another hazard. For combat operations, military mountaineers may need to compromise on protection and belays even further. Speed, stealth, and the ability to react are critical if enemy contact is expected. SECTION IV - TOP ROPE CLIMBING 10-33. A top rope is a belay in which both rope ends are on the ground and the rope runs up to the top of the cliff (or climb) and passes through a pre-established anchor point. This enables one Soldier to climb while the other Soldier belays. The belayer keeps the rope tight to prevent the climber from falling more than

to the top of the cliff (or climb) and passes through a pre-established anchor point. This enables one Soldier to climb while the other Soldier belays. The belayer keeps the rope tight to prevent the climber from falling more than a short distance. This system also enables the belayer to lower the climber back down to the ground after completing the climb. (See figure 10-7 for an example of top rope climbing.) 244 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Rope Systems for Climbing Figure 10-7. Top rope climbing 10-34. A top rope is a training tool. It allows Soldiers to learn the fundamentals of tying in and belaying and to practice individual climbing techniques without the consequences of a long leader fall or unroped fall. It allows one instructor to coach and supervise both the climber and the belayer. It also facilitates learning the climbing technique because all participants can observe one another. EQUIPMENT CONSIDERATIONS 10-35. The UIAA develops safety and testing standards for mountaineering equipment. Equipment used for any mountaineering training should meet these standards as outlined in chapter 8 and appendix C. HELMETS 10-36. Helmets will protect a Soldier from rockfall and debris. They also offer some protection from impacts in a swinging fall. Climbing helmets are lightweight and certified to standards set by the UIAA. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 245

Chapter 10 10-37. Most units do not have access to climbing helmets. The combat helmet, while not rated or designed for impact protection from rockfall or in climbing falls, is already issued to most Soldiers and provides adequate protection. HARNESS 10-38. There are many types of climbing harnesses. Harnesses must be made and tested to UIAA standards, and users must ensure that wear and use conforms to manufacturer recommendations. The high-angle mountaineering kit (HAMK) is issued to units where most Soldiers have no formal mountaineering training. The harness that was selected for the HAMK (see figure 10-8), is a harness with a single, reinforced tie-in portion. It is a simpler harness than most recreational climbing harnesses. It is one-size fits all and easy to put on and inspect. It has one gear loop on the left side, which can be used to rack equipment. When worn, it should be tight around the waist, with the leg loops snug enough to take some of the force while falling or sitting into the harness. 10-39. take some of the force while falling or sitting into the harness. 10-39. If harnesses are not available, tubular webbing can be used to make field expedient harnesses, although this is not preferred. Soldiers must ensure their seats are tied correctly, and military mountaineers acting as safeties must carefully inspect several more points. Dynamic ropes stretch and reduce the peak impact force felt by a climber in a fall. Falls while top roping should not generate as much force as a lead fall; however, if slack develops in the belay, such as from a stuck rope or slow belayer, there is potential for generating significant force. 10-42. Top rope training puts significant wear and tear on ropes. New climbers fall often, and because a rope may be used on the same climb for the entire day, there may be significant wear in the same sections of rope. Heavy-duty climbing ropes in the 10-mm range are recommended for top rope training. The 10.2-mm dynamic rope included in the ACTKs provides good durability. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 247

Chapter 10 PREPARATION 10-43. Advanced and master military mountaineers should plan and supervise mountaineering training that involves roped climbing and rappelling. They advise the commander on training requirements, priorities, and equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training. SITE RECONNAISSANCE 10-44. Visit the training area before the scheduled training date and conduct a rehearsal or walkthrough with key personnel. This will help proof the plan, identify hazards, and develop controls. It is also an opportunity to save time with set up by identifying anchors and cleaning the area of loose rock or other hazards ahead of time. TIME MANAGEMENT 10-45. Ensure the training plan provides ample time to cover movement, set up, demonstrations, and training time. Extra time for contingencies is often needed. COMMUNICATION 10-46. All key personnel should have reliable communication with each other to communicate changes to hazards or conditions or to coordinate the response to emergencies. PARTICIPANT-TO-INSTRUCTOR RATIO 10-47. Ensure an adequate number of trained personnel are available to effectively supervise the given number of participants. ORGANIZATION OR PLACEMENT OF KEY PERSONNEL 10-48. Critical points must be identified, and key personnel must be placed or distributed to facilitate supervision of the training site. EMERGENCY AND MEDICAL EVACUATION PLANS 10-49. Emergency and MEDEVAC plans must include special equipment and must consider the nature of the terrain in the training area. These plans must be rehearsed to ensure the viability of the plan. TRAINING SITE CONSIDERATION 10-50. The following are important considerations when managing a top rope training site. EASE OF ACCESS 10-51. The top of the cliff must be accessible to safely establish the anchors and hang ropes. Otherwise, a climb may have to be led prior to rigging. The bottom of the cliff must be easily accessible for the group and have adequate space to safely move around and store equipment. LENGTH OF CLIMBS 10-52. The length of the climbs must be less than half the length of the available ropes. Longer climbs can

be easily accessible for the group and have adequate space to safely move around and store equipment. LENGTH OF CLIMBS 10-52. The length of the climbs must be less than half the length of the available ropes. Longer climbs can be used by joining two ropes together but is more complex and should be avoided, if possible, when working with beginners. DIFFICULTY 10-53. Ensure the difficulty of climbing is appropriate for the Soldiers. A common mistake is to use climbs that are too difficult for Soldiers to learn the basic movement skills and establish confidence. It is best to have a variety of difficulty levels available. 248 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Rope Systems for Climbing DISTANCE BETWEEN CLIMBS 10-54. Climbs should be far enough apart so that climbers are not falling on or swinging into other climbers; however, they should not be so far apart that supervision and control are hindered. With climbs in close proximity, the instructor can often maintain adequate supervision of more than one climb. TRAINING SITE ANCHORS 10-55. Anchors at training sites are built stronger and more redundant than others used in climbing. A top roping anchor is used for long durations of time and is often out of the user's sight. It either is loaded frequently, with climbers falling or as each climber is lowered back down to the ground. Extra care should be taken to avoid sharp edges and add padding where necessary. LOCATION OF ANCHORS 10-56. Anchors should be located directly above the climb. If the anchor is not above the climb, during a fall climbers will pendulum, swinging across the face until they are in line with the anchor. This is more pronounced the closer to the top the climber gets. CONSTRUCTION OF ANCHORS 10-57. Anchors must be strong and redundant. Developed climbing areas often have bolted anchors at the top of climbs.

Developed climbing areas often have bolted anchors at the top of climbs. A top roping anchor can be built with these with a cord as for other applications. (See figure 10-9.) Locking carabiners may be substituted for non-locking carabiners to ensure that the anchor is secure, even if it is checked only a few times during the training day. If anchors are unavailable at the cliff edge or are not in line with the top of the climb, static rope can be used to extend anchors out over the edge of the cliff and create a master point that is in line. Anchor ropes should be at least 9.5 mm in diameter. Figure 10-9. Top rope climbing set up INSPECTIONS 10-58. The site should be organized in such a way that participants are unable to climb or proceed towards edges or dangerous terrain without first being inspected. Trainers must have a clear, logical sequence to follow when conducting inspections, whether it is anchor points, harnesses, tie-ins, rappel hook ups, or other. These should be conducted hands-on, not viewed from a distance. TOP ROPE BELAY 10-59. Top rope training develops two main skills. One is the individual mobility skill of the climber. The other is belaying. Belaying is the most important for safe training. POSITIONING THE BELAYER 10-60. The best position to catch a fall is directly below the anchor. The belayer will be pulled straight up and not off-balance. However, belayers should be offset enough so that the climber will not fall on them. They should also be positioned so that the rope will not interfere with climbers as they climb the route or entangle the climber in the event of a fall. The belayer should be protected from hazards, such as falling rock or ice. They should be placed into a protected feature under a roof or bulge or offset out

route or entangle the climber in the event of a fall. The belayer should be protected from hazards, such as falling rock or ice. They should be placed into a protected feature under a roof or bulge or offset out of the path of any falling objects. ANCHORING THE BELAYER 10-61. Anchoring belayers can keep them from being pulled off their stance during a fall. It is not always necessary, but the decision not to anchor should be deliberate. It is recommended that the belayer is anchored when- * Belayers are inexperienced and may lose control of the belay if they are pulled up. * The climber severely outweighs the belayer. * It is necessary to keep them from being pulled into hazards and obstructions. BACK-UP BELAYER 10-62. Using back-up belayers can achieve several things. Back-up belayers improve the overall security of the climbers, since it decreases the likelihood that a Soldier could be dropped to the ground. Back-up belayers help to convey the importance of the belay when learning is first taking place and keeps additional Soldiers occupied and focused when unit trainers are working with large numbers of participants. To provide a back-up belay, one Soldier stands just behind the primary belayer, on the brake-hand side, and keeps additional control of the rope while making sure not to interfere with the primary belayer's movements. The device, plus the belayer's braking hand, keeps tension on the rope in the event of a fall and helps protect the climber at the other end. It is an essential device for climbing safety. 10-64. Tube-style devices are the most used belay devices. (See figure 10-10.) They are lightweight, simple, and do not twist the rope. The brake position with a tube-style device is down, with the brake hand below the device, creating two sharp bends in the rope that provide the necessary friction. Its main disadvantage is that it twists and kinks the rope. * Place a locking carabiner into the tie-in portion of the harness. Lock the carabiner. * To take in rope, grasp the brake strand with the brake hand a few inches away from the Munter hitch and with the thumb pointed up. Using standardized verbal climbing commands is a necessary safety protocol to ensure both members are ready before any actions are taken. Commands while top roping also teach proper communication before introducing lead climbing, where communication may occur over a much longer distance. Clear communication minimizes the chance of human error and helps to ensure safe operation of the belay. All commands must be preceded by the other Soldier's first or last name, like a radio transmission, to gain the other Soldier's attention. This is especially important at training sites where there are multiple top rope climbs set up nearby to avoid confusion. 10-67. Units and schoolhouses should develop their own SOPs to determine appropriate commands. Consider the following when choosing these terms: * Avoid using terms that sound alike or may be confused with another word (for example, GO, SLOW, and WHOAH may sound like NO and vice versa). * Avoid using words that are not definitive (for example, GOOD is a vague term that does not define any specific action). 10-68. The procedures for conducting a lead climb with a group of two are relatively simple. The most experienced individual is the lead climber or leader. Leaders are responsible for selecting the route. They must ensure that the route is well within their climbing ability and that of the second climber ("second"). The lead climber carries most of the climbing equipment to place protection along the route and set up the next belay. The leader must also ensure that the second has the necessary equipment, such as a chock pick, to remove any protection that the leader may place. 10-91. The leader is responsible for emplacing protection frequently enough and in such a manner that if either the leader or the second should fall, their fall is neither long enough nor hard enough to result in injury. The other member of the climbing team, the second, is responsible for belaying the leader, removing the belay anchor, and retrieving the protection placed by the leader between belay positions (also known as cleaning the pitch). 10-93. Generally, protection is placed from one stable position to the next. If the climbing is difficult, protection should be placed more frequently. No matter how direct the route, the climber often encounters problems with rope drag through the protection positions. Rope drag is caused when there are exaggerated changes in direction of the rope between carabiners attached to protection that creates excessive friction. Minimal rope drag is an inconvenience; severe rope drag may pull the climber off balance, inducing a fall. When belaying the second, rope drag can be mistaken for the climber, causing the belayer to not take in the necessary slack. This can potentially result in a serious fall. To prevent this, the placements should be extended by using runners, when necessary, so the rope creates a smooth, almost straight line as it passes through the carabiners. (See figure 10-16.) Do this by attaching an appropriate-length runner to the protection to extend the rope connection in the necessary direction. Rope Systems for Climbing On Ledges 10-110. On small or large ledges, it is usually possible to stack the rope in a neat pile as it is pulled through the belay. This allows for an easy transition and for smooth rope feeding. At Hanging Stances 10-111. At hanging belay stances, it may be necessary to stack the rope back and forth over the tie-in strand as the Soldier pulls rope through the belay. If this is done, the rope should be looped back and forth in large bights (not so long as to becoming caught on things below). If the second becomes the new leader for the next pitch, these bights should start big and gradually become smaller. This allows the rope to feed out without becoming tangled during the next lead. If the original leader leads the next pitch, the rope may have to be restacked over the second's tie-in strand when they reach the anchor. Another option is to stack the rope back and forth over a leg or foot. Sometimes yelling cannot be heard when the climber and belayer are far apart. They advise the commander on training requirements, priorities, and equipment needs, as well as plan, organize, and conduct training. Lead climbing training is particularly demanding of trainers and supervisors. For inexperienced climbers, a 2:1 ratio is often required. Supervision of climbing training must be thorough and deliberate. A large part of this supervision is inspecting every component of the rope system. Chapter 10 SECTION VI - ALPINE BELAY TECHNIQUES 10-118. In broken alpine terrain, with secure stances, and no chance of second climbers falling and hanging from a belay, hasty techniques may provide adequate protection for the team. Safety should never be compromised for the sake of speed. Use of standard belay techniques should be used if there is any question as to security. BODY BELAYS 10-119. Body belays can sometimes be used on short sections of less steep terrain where a fall is unlikely and there is a good, braced belay stance of which to take advantage. To create a body belay, simply run the rope around the body at the waist to create friction, with the chest facing the direction of pull. The load rope is at one hip and the brake strand is in the opposite side hand. To take in rope, pull in on the load rope with the guide hand and out with the brake hand. Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the

Grab both ropes above the brake hand with the guide hand and slide the brake hand back towards the body. To brake, pull the brake hand up and across the chest. The body belay can be used in either the sitting or standing position; however, the sitting position offers a lower center of gravity and is preferred. It can also be used with an anchor or without. The advantage of the body belay is its speed and simplicity for belaying short sections where a climber is moving quickly. However, there are disadvantages as well. Because the force of a fall is dissipated as friction against belayers' bodies, serious rope burns can occur to the body and hands, possibly causing them to lose control of the belay. It also generates less braking force and causes more slippage than other techniques, causing the climber to fall farther. For this reason, it is only used on low-angle easy terrain. The belayer must have a good, braced position and must keep the rope tight. (See figure 10-21.) 268 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Rope Systems for Climbing Figure 10-21. Hip belay SHOULDER BELAY 10-120. A shoulder belay is a way to add a level of friction to the rope as the belayer pulls it tight with a climber below. The shoulder belay shares many of the advantages and disadvantages listed above for the body belay. The level of friction created with this method is relatively low and should only be used on short steps where there is no risk of the climber hanging from the belay in a fall. A classic example of terrain where the shoulder belay is appropriate is a short, steep step where the belayer can stand directly above the climber below. The rope is routed under the arm, over the opposite shoulder, and down to the opposite hand and is kept tight with the climber below. The belayer's body creates friction on the rope and acts as the anchor at the same time. A shoulder belay is fast to create, but it is only suitable on rare occasions. (See figure 10-22, page 270.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 269

Chapter 10 Figure 10-22. Shoulder belay 10-121. A terrain belay can be used when there is a feature that the rope can go around and create enough friction to arrest a fall or lower a load. The natural feature must be solid and not have sharp edges. Terrain belays are an effective means of belaying a climbing partner, but they require good judgement. When using a boulder or horn of rock, the belayer must ensure the rope will not slide off the rock in the event of a fall and that the rock is wedged securely. Trees are another good example of a natural object that can be used as a terrain belay. (See chapter 9 for more information on tree selection.) (See figure 10-23.) 270 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

There are numerous examples of when it may be beneficial to work and move as a team of three. Moving as a team of three has added complexity and much more challenging rope management at each belay. To progress into managing two ropes, a climber must first become proficient in managing one. 10-123. It is good for military mountaineers to have options for roped travel through terrain with changing hazards. The mountaineer must constantly assess terrain and hazards and fluidly adapt the technique to mitigate those hazards as best as possible. Time is always against mountaineers, and efficient transitions from one roped movement style to the next are important. A mountaineer should not default to using one style of movement for all types of terrain and should know how to properly apply different roped movement techniques to different terrain. Having second climbers ascend rather than climb removes any possibility of a second not being able to reach the top due to a lack of climbing ability. The second would then ascend the rope rather than climb on belay. It is not appropriate in all terrain due to various terrain hazards. The weighted rope can dislodge loose rock. The rope is easily damaged or cut if it runs over a sharp edge while the followers ascend. (See chapter 11 for more information on ascending ropes.) 274 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Chapter 11 Fixed Ropes Fixed ropes are an important part of military mountaineering as they facilitate the movement of Soldiers through rugged terrain. Fixed ropes allow large groups of Soldiers to safely access terrain that provides tactical advantage over the enemy. They have proven useful in past conflicts. During World War II, they were successfully used during Operation Neptune (commonly referred to as D-day) and the famous assault on Riva Ridge by the 10th Mountain Division. Proficiency in using fixed ropes allows units to overcome mobility limitations and, therefore, achieve greater lethality in mountainous terrain. SECTION I - BASIC FIXED-ROPE TECHNIQUES 11-1. A fixed rope is any rope system attached to at least one anchor that can be used to improve security and efficiency of movement through difficult terrain that subjects Soldiers to a fall hazard. They can be used for ascending, descending, or traversing across steep terrain in which a fall hazard exists. They may simply provide Soldiers with a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to fall. They can be used to assist the movement

a handhold through a short section of steep terrain or as complex as hundreds of feet of broken hazardous terrain involving numerous sections that prevent attached Soldiers from being able to fall. They can be used to assist the movement of small teams to large units. They allow units to overcome mobility limitations and access tactically advantageous terrain. FIXED-ROPE CONSIDERATIONS 11-2. Fixed ropes should be used whenever a group of Soldiers cannot move safely through a section of terrain unroped. Fixed ropes are usually the most efficient means of protecting groups larger than team sized, especially if the groups have not received advanced military mountaineering training. Common factors contributing to the necessity of building fixed ropes are fall hazard, slippery surfaces, limited visibility, heavy loads, low mobility skills, and fatigue. 11-3. The two basic types of fixed-rope systems are simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate anchors. Both types have applications in every class of terrain. Simple fixed ropes are anchored only at the top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top. Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more

are anchored only at the top, can only be used by one Soldier at a time, and require a straight path of movement from bottom to top. Fixed ropes with intermediate anchors have multiple anchors and rope sections, allowing more Soldiers to move on them simultaneously and the path to change directions. Each type is determined by route and availability of anchors along it, the number of Soldiers to use the system, and the type of available equipment to attach to it. 11-4. All types of fixed ropes are built from the top down over, or through, terrain obstacles. However, fixed rope installation teams may need to ascend terrain using other techniques prior to building a fixed-rope system. (See chapter 10.) 11-5. Units planning to use fixed ropes must establish installation teams capable of locating routes, moving safely through various terrain obstacles, and building a variety of installations. They should be led by advanced military mountaineers but may be assisted by basic military mountaineers. These teams should be experienced in building fixed ropes in the type of terrain to be negotiated, equipped appropriately for the task, and familiar with the capabilities of the Soldiers who use them. 11-6. These teams should be experienced in building fixed ropes in the type of terrain to be negotiated, equipped appropriately for the task, and familiar with the capabilities of the Soldiers who use them. 11-6. In a tactical environment, any terrain that requires a fixed rope should be considered a VDA, which is steep terrain that puts a unit moving through it at significant tactical disadvantage. The process for establishing even the simplest fixed rope comes at the cost of time and exposure to enemy attack. Adequate security must be established prior to deploying the installation team. In complex terrain, security teams may need to be adjusted or leap-frogged forward if fixed-rope systems cover large pieces of terrain. Emplacing security teams in a complex terrain may require high-mobility skills as well as substantial time. Typically, it is best to approach fixed-rope terrain from above because security is more easily established on higher 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 275

SIMPLE FIXED ROPES 11-7. A simple fixed rope is a rope that is anchored at the top of steep terrain that can be used to increase safety or efficiency of movement up or down. The method of anchoring the rope is determined by anchor features available but can be as simple as a bowline tied to a tree or as complex as a multipoint anchor established with rock-climbing gear. The principal benefit of simple, fixed ropes is their simplicity and speed of construction. 11-8. Simple fixed ropes are typically established by one mountaineer climbing the obstacle, dragging a rope, and then anchoring it at the top. They can also be established by approaching the top of a steep obstacle by some other means, anchoring a rope, and lowering the other end down for others to use. 11-9. Some important considerations for using simple fixed-rope systems are that they must follow a path straight up the terrain feature, the attachment technique is appropriate to reduce fall risk, and they allow for

end down for others to use. 11-9. Some important considerations for using simple fixed-rope systems are that they must follow a path straight up the terrain feature, the attachment technique is appropriate to reduce fall risk, and they allow for a large enough loading and unloading platform to manage the site safely. Using a friction hitch or mechanical progress capture to attach to the rope provides increased security during movement. EASY TERRAIN 11-10. Short 2nd- or 3rd-class slopes with low fall consequence can be negotiated using simple fixed ropes without the necessity of attaching to the rope. Soldiers using the fixed rope simply grasp the rope with the thumb downward and use it in a hand-over-hand fashion to assist with balance. (See figure 11-1.) This technique is appropriate when there is an increased likelihood of fall but low consequence. Usually this means short slopes that Soldiers could easily negotiate normally, but slippery conditions, fatigue, or heavy loads increase the chance of a fall. Knots can be added to increase the security of Soldiers moving on the rope, making it less likely their hand slips on the rope. Figure 11-1. Simple fixed rope use in easy terrain 276 TC 3-97.61 26

Fixed Ropes MODERATE TERRAIN 11-11. Short sections of steep 3rd or 4th class with higher fall consequence can be negotiated by attaching to simple fixed ropes with a progress capture, such as a prusik or other mechanical rope-grabbing device. This technique requires Soldiers to wear some type of harness. A significant drawback to this technique is that it takes a lot of time to move a group of Soldiers. Only one Soldier can move at a time on a rope, and time is lost during attachment and detachment. (See figure 11-2, page 278.) Prusik Technique 11-12. A common technique involves tying a prusik on the rope with a cordelette, then tying a fixed loop in the other end of the two tails. Clip the fixed loop to the harness with a locking carabiner. The optimum length of the attachment is one outstretched arm. 11-13. Ascend the fixed rope by using the legs to climb the slope and the rope as a handhold for balance, sliding the prusik up to capture progress and prevent fall in case of a slip. 11-14. The prusik technique is recommended only on simple fixed ropes without intermediate anchor points because friction hitches cannot be easily

a handhold for balance, sliding the prusik up to capture progress and prevent fall in case of a slip. 11-14. The prusik technique is recommended only on simple fixed ropes without intermediate anchor points because friction hitches cannot be easily or safely transitioned past intermediate anchors. Mechanical Ascender Technique 11-15. It is also possible to use a rope-grabbing device, such as a mechanical ascender, to create a progress capture for Soldiers moving on fixed ropes. These devices are easier and faster to use but require every Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has limited uses. They should be used when fixed rope ascents are planned for large groups in moderate terrain. 11-16. Mechanical ascenders are devices shaped like a handle that can be attached to a rope by means of a toothed cam. It can slide in one direction on a rope but not the other. When weighted, the camming mechanism activates and grips the rope. Soldiers can attach ascenders to their harness and slide them along fixed ropes during movement, capturing their progress and preventing a fall during a slip (see figure 11-2, page 278). Ascenders should never be dynamically loaded as their teeth could damage the

attach ascenders to their harness and slide them along fixed ropes during movement, capturing their progress and preventing a fall during a slip (see figure 11-2, page 278). Ascenders should never be dynamically loaded as their teeth could damage the rope. Ascenders are included in the Army ACTK, but Solders can use other similar ascenders to ascend fixed ropes. Some are much lighter but are less easy to use. Advanced military mountaineers should familiarize themselves with the options available and units should obtain those best suited to the mountaineering tasks they must perform. 11-17. To use a mechanical ascender, attach it to the fixed rope. Then girth hitch a sling to the harness and clip it to the ascender with a locking carabiner. (See figure 11-2, page 278.) 11-18. Ascend the fixed rope by using the legs to climb the slope and the ascender as a handhold for balance, sliding it up to capture progress and prevent fall in the case of a slip. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 277

Chapter 11 Figure 11-2. Simple fixed-rope attachments in moderate terrain VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-19. Moving on simple fixed ropes in terrain where significant sections are very steep or vertical requires rigging that is more complex. These rigging techniques provide secure attachment to the rope and aid movement up the rope. (See paragraphs 11-36 through 11-52, pages 282 through 286, for more information on ascending techniques.) FIXED ROPES WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS 11-20. Larger or more complex sections of steep terrain require fixed ropes with intermediate anchors to ensure adequate safety and efficiency of movement. This may involve various sections of 3rd, 4th, or even 5th-class terrain. The principal difference between simple fixed ropes and fixed ropes with intermediate anchors is the use of intermediate anchor points to create independent sections and changes in direction of travel. This allows the movement route to follow the easiest, safest, and most efficient path. This type of fixed rope is commonly used along exposed ridges and narrow mountain passes. 11-21. Advanced or master military mountaineers with substantial experience are required to establish fixed ropes with intermediate anchors, but they can be assisted by basic military mountaineers. FIXED-ROPE CONSTRUCTION WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS 11-22. The primary guiding principles

narrow mountain passes. 11-21. Advanced or master military mountaineers with substantial experience are required to establish fixed ropes with intermediate anchors, but they can be assisted by basic military mountaineers. FIXED-ROPE CONSTRUCTION WITH INTERMEDIATE ANCHORS 11-22. The primary guiding principles for building a fixed rope with intermediate anchors are that they provide adequate fall prevention while maximizing the speed at which Soldiers can move using them. Path 11-23. Establishing a fixed rope with intermediate anchors starts with thorough terrain analysis and route finding. When selecting a path for the rope, mountaineers must consider the anchor options available, difficulty of movement on the route, and any other objective hazards present. The characteristics of the Soldiers who use the fixed rope are also useful information. Particularly, what their mobility and technical skill levels are and what equipment they have for attaching to the rope. 278 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Intermediate Anchors 11-24. Terrain and vegetation determine the equipment mountaineers need to build the fixed rope. Heavily vegetated terrain or broken rocky terrain may only require cordelettes, slings, and carabiners. Slabby or steep rock faces require cams, nuts, and other lead climbing protection to build anchors. Intermediate anchors must be built robust enough to support the weight of a fall by the number of Soldiers who will move on each section at a given time. When possible, anchors should be built at about waist height in places where good footing is possible so that transitioning past anchors is easier for Soldiers moving on the fixed rope (See figure 11-3 for common methods of attaching ropes to single component anchors.) Rope Section Slack 11-25. Fixed-rope sections do not have a standard amount of slack. There should be enough slack to allow Soldiers to follow the easiest path through terrain without adding fall risk. Sometimes a lot of slack is necessary to go around an obstacle or steep section. This is usually better than running a tighter rope over these things, because going around is easier, which reduces the chance of a fall. Other times, a section may need to

necessary to go around an obstacle or steep section. This is usually better than running a tighter rope over these things, because going around is easier, which reduces the chance of a fall. Other times, a section may need to be tight to reduce fall distance, such as traversing across a cliff on a narrow ledge. Figure 11-3. Intermediate anchors in moderate terrain, example ATTACHMENT AND MOVEMENT 11-26. The method for movement on fixed ropes with intermediate anchors is as important as how they are constructed. Two primary methods exist for use in steep terrain: the two personal safeties method and the ascender-carabiner method. Choosing between the two is a tradeoff between not carrying heavier single-purpose items and having more security during movement. The two personal safeties method requires no special equipment but cannot eliminate fall risk for a Soldier. The ascender-carabiner method prevents falling but requires each Soldier to carry a piece of equipment that has little other use. Both techniques have their place, and both must be considered for use when planning fixed-rope movements. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 279

Chapter 11 Two Personal Safeties Method 11-27. This method involves having two separate girth hitched slings attached to the tie-in portion of the harness with a single nonlocking carabiner in each. The carabiners are then attached to the fixed rope. Always keep the two carabiners attached to the rope unless they move past an intermediate anchor. To move past an intermediate anchor, clip one carabiner at a time above the anchor. When both carabiners are above the anchor, continue movement. (See figure 11-4.) 11-28. The two personal safeties method is appropriate for situations where the fall consequence is high, but the likelihood is low. It can be used up to 4th-class terrain under good conditions (such as good surface conditions, moderate mobility skills, light loads, well-rested, high visibility) provided that intermediate anchors are appropriately spaced to prevent serious fall injury. Since falls using this method are only stopped by the last anchor a Soldier passed, there is always a chance of injury. This should be considered carefully before choosing it. Figure 11-4. Two personal safeties attachment 280 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Ascender-Carabiner Method 11-29. The ascender-carabiner method is the fastest and most secure way to travel up very steep fixed ropes. It is preferred when fall risk is substantial or sections of the fixed rope are long, because the ascender captures the Soldiers' progress as they move. 11-30. To use this technique, girth hitch two slings into the harness. Clip one nonlocking carabiner into one extension. Clip a mechanical ascender to the other extension with a locking carabiner. 11-31. Ascend in the same manner as with simple fixed ropes. To move past the intermediate anchor, clip the nonlocking carabiner above the anchor, and then move the ascender to above the carabiner on the fixed rope. (See figure 11-5.) 11-32. This method is appropriate when both fall consequence and likelihood are high. It can be used in terrain up to 4th class under any conditions. It is the best method when surface conditions are slippery, loads are heavy, mobility skills are low or Soldiers are fatigued, during low visibility, and when intermediate anchors cannot be established to prevent fall injury. Figure 11-5. Ascender-carabiner method 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 281

Chapter 11 FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-33. Fixed ropes are sometimes necessary for moving in vertical terrain during complex rescue operations or other special operations in permissive or nontactical environments. They are rarely practical for tactical operations, given their extreme exposure to enemy observation and direct fire. However, vertical terrain is not always avoidable during combat operations, and there are historical examples of their use during pivotal cliff assaults. Vertical terrain is the most extreme example of VDA. Soldiers moving on vertically fixed ropes require well-established overwatch security since they are totally exposed and can do little but ascend the fixed rope. 11-34. Moving on fixed ropes in vertical terrain requires Soldiers to possess the equipment and skills necessary to ascend rope, relying entirely on their attachment to it to prevent fall. Efficient ascending requires specialized equipment. CONSTRUCTING FIXED ROPES IN VERTICAL TERRAIN 11-35. Fixed ropes in vertical terrain are constructed in the same fashion as moderate terrain; however, they take greater technical rope skills, experience with complex anchoring, and time to establish. With fixed ropes in moderate terrain, it would be ideal for the installation team to approach the route from the top and build the system top-down.

they take greater technical rope skills, experience with complex anchoring, and time to establish. With fixed ropes in moderate terrain, it would be ideal for the installation team to approach the route from the top and build the system top-down. However, this is rarely possible. Typically, they must be established from the bottom up by advanced military mountaineers employing lead climbing techniques to get the rope to the top. This process is time-consuming and inherently risky. ASCENDING TECHNIQUES 11-36. Many situations may require a Soldier to ascend a rope in very steep or vertical terrain. Soldiers must be prepared and equipped to do so when operating in 4th- and 5th-class terrain. Typically, ascending rope is a more efficient technique than climbing for moving followers over hard climbing terrain, to include those members of small assault climber teams. 11-37. The techniques described below are for single strands of rope, so it is imperative that appropriate measures are taken to pad the rope near sharp edges. Whenever Soldiers plan to ascend vertical terrain, they should use mechanical ascenders to achieve maximum safety and efficiency during movement. 11-38. Ascending techniques are also key skills used in rescue operations, self-rescue during crevasse fall, and

rope near sharp edges. Whenever Soldiers plan to ascend vertical terrain, they should use mechanical ascenders to achieve maximum safety and efficiency during movement. 11-38. Ascending techniques are also key skills used in rescue operations, self-rescue during crevasse fall, and whenever rappellers find their rope does not reach the ground. Prusik Ascent 11-39. Two prusiks can be used to ascend rope. One prusik is tied to the fixed rope using a cordelette at approximately forehead height. A fixed loop is tied in the hanging tails to create an attachment point at about waist level. This is then secured to the harness with a locking carabiner. Another prusik is tied to the fixed rope at about waist level. The hanging tails are then tied to one or both feet using any appropriate knot to form a foot stirrup. (See figure 11-6.) 11-40. The upper prusik serves as the "progress capture," during ascent, by holding the Soldier up, while the lower friction hitch serves as the "progress" or makeshift foothold. During movement, the lower hitch is slid up as high as possible while hanging from the upper hitch. Soldiers then stand up on the lower hitch, pushing down and behind them with

hitch serves as the "progress" or makeshift foothold. During movement, the lower hitch is slid up as high as possible while hanging from the upper hitch. Soldiers then stand up on the lower hitch, pushing down and behind them with their leg, while sliding the upper hitch as high as possible. They then rest in the harness from the upper hitch and continue. Safety knots should be tied in the fixed rope below the lower hitch and attached to the harness with a locking carabiner every 10 to 15 feet. This provides a backup against failure of the friction hitch to grab. This technique should be considered an improvised technique for use when ascending is not expected. 282 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-6. Prusik ascent Prusik Ascender Method 11-41. Mechanical ascenders are a one-directional device used to capture progress along a rope and assist climbers as they ascend steep, vertical, or free-hanging terrain. They can be substituted for one or both hitches described in prusik ascent. They make ascending efficient and fast. 11-42. To use an ascender as a progress capture, attach it to the rope at about head height. Girth hitch a sling or cordelette to the harness, and then use a locking carabiner to secure the other end to the bottom of the ascender, forming an arm-length extension between them. Commonly, a nonlocking carabiner is clipped around the rope through the top of the ascender for added security. This prevents the device from twisting off the rope. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 283

Chapter 11 11-43. To create the progress with an ascender, attach it to the rope at about waist height. Girth hitch or use any carabiner to attach a sling or cordelette to the bottom of the carabiner and tie it to one or both feet using any appropriate knot. The movement process is the same as described above for prusik ascent. 11-44. There are dozens of devices available that work the same as an ascender. Ensure the rope type and diameter are appropriate for the device used, as most mechanical devices have a specified range of acceptable use. Read all manufacturers' instructions to ensure safe use. 11-45. Stopper knots should be tied in the fixed rope below the lower hitch or device and attached to the harness with a locking carabiner every 10 to 15 feet. This provides a backup against the rope grabs slipping. This technique should be used when ascending is planned but not enough ascenders are available for Soldiers to be issued two. Double-Ascender Method 11-46. This technique is extremely efficient once it has been practiced. It is a recommended technique for ascending long distances. An etrier or cordelette forming a foot stirrup is hung off each

for Soldiers to be issued two. Double-Ascender Method 11-46. This technique is extremely efficient once it has been practiced. It is a recommended technique for ascending long distances. An etrier or cordelette forming a foot stirrup is hung off each ascender with a locking carabiner. Both ascenders are then placed on the rope. A cordelette or sling also hangs off each ascender and is girth hitched to the user's harness, creating two attachment points to the rope. (See figure 11-7.) 11-47. To use the system, the Soldier places a foot in each etrier (or stirrup) and slides the upper ascender up the rope. This upper ascender is easier to move because the Soldier's weight is on the lower ascender. The lower ascender is moved up next, while the upper ascender supports the Soldier's weight. Sometimes it is necessary to slightly release the camming mechanism before moving an ascender. 11-48. It is also recommended to tie back-up knots periodically in the same manner as prusik ascent. 11-49. This technique is the most efficient and is recommended for use whenever ascending is a planned movement technique. 284 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-7. Double-ascender ascent SPECIAL TECHNIQUES AND CONSIDERATIONS 11-50. There are too many considerations for using and improving fixed ropes to cover them all in this training circular. However, the following techniques should be considered for use with fixed ropes. Weapon Management 11-51. Unless enemy attack is imminent, weapons should be slung to the rear, allowing Soldiers to scramble more easily in difficult terrain. Heavier weapons, such as sniper weapon systems, mortars, and machine guns, may need to be attached to the top of rucksacks. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 285

Chapter 11 Improving Steps 11-52. Soldiers are less likely to fall and move more quickly if they have good footing. Hard snow is especially easy to carve steps into and can allow Soldiers to move with less exertion on their calf muscles. Carving steps should be done first in steeper sections and, as time allows, in other areas too. Platforms can also be made where Soldiers are transitioning past intermediate anchors. If a Soldier can easily stand near an intermediate anchor, they can clip around it much faster. This greatly lessens the time required for the group to navigate terrain where objective hazards may be present. Etriers or Slings at Difficult Steps 11-53. The hanging of a sling or etrier (for use as a hand or foothold) where there is a difficult step can help reduce fall potential and increase speed of the group. An etrier is a short ladder that can be made from any piece of rope or cord and creates an artificial step in a place where there is no natural feature to step on. The etrier can be hung off an intermediate anchor or its own anchor. (See figure 11-8.) Caving Ladders 11-54. Manufactured ladders can

cord and creates an artificial step in a place where there is no natural feature to step on. The etrier can be hung off an intermediate anchor or its own anchor. (See figure 11-8.) Caving Ladders 11-54. Manufactured ladders can be useful for large steps and crevasse negotiation. They also enable Soldiers to navigate challenging terrain in the dark, much easier than if they had to search for hand and foot placements. Some are constructed of materials that can be rolled up for transport. While they may make the ascent of a blank wall easier, they are cumbersome to carry. Cables and Via-Ferrata 11-55. If terrain is to be repetitively used for access to higher points for something semi-permanent such as an observation post, it may be in the unit's best interest to build a via-ferrata style system for access. A via-ferrata works similarly to a fixed rope with intermediate anchors, except it uses cable instead of rope. Using cable reduces the need for constant inspection and greatly increases durability. They are much more time consuming to build, but it may be the most feasible option if a unit uses a piece of terrain for an extended period. Given the

They are much more time consuming to build, but it may be the most feasible option if a unit uses a piece of terrain for an extended period. Given the cable's rigidity, the attachment method used by Soldiers needs to provide the stretch to lessen fall forces. This equipment can be found on the civilian market. Another component of a via-ferrata-style system is the addition of metal ladder style and foot and handholds. These are for areas and routes that will see traffic over a long time, making the use of soft materials impractical. 286 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Figure 11-8. Etrier styles SECTION II - TYPES OF RAPPELLING 11-56. Rappelling is a method of descending steep terrain using a rope and a means of creating friction to control the rate of descent. This provides Soldiers with a safe way to descend terrain that would otherwise expose them to very high fall risks. 11-57. If the descent distance is greater than a rope length (for example, multipitch), multiple, simple fixed lines can be linked together with anchors at the top and bottom of each rope. Soldiers can then rappel from anchor to anchor and transition from rope to rope until they reach the ground. This method requires many resources and numerous personnel to establish and manage safely. 11-58. Small teams with fewer resources must use the one or two ropes they can carry to rappel the whole group from one anchor to a lower one, then retrieve the rope, and repeat the process until the ground is reached. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 287

Chapter 11 RAPPELLING FUNDAMENTALS 11-59. Rappelling is a quick method of descent, but it can be extremely dangerous. The dangers include anchor failure, equipment failure, and individual error. Carefully select anchors in a mountainous environment. In a mountain environment, take great care to load the anchor slowly and to ensure that no excessive stress is placed on the anchor. To ensure this, prohibit bounding while rappelling; Soldiers should slowly descend. Soldiers should avoid dragging their feet when moving backwards towards the edge as this causes rockfall. 11-60. Soldiers rappelling with weapons should sling them on the back or to the side when wearing packs. Soldiers carrying particularly heavy weapons, such as machine guns, sniper rifles, or mortars may need to strap them to the top of their pack and use additional techniques described below to make rappelling less difficult. RAPPEL SITE SELECTION 11-61. Selecting the rappel point depends on factors, such as mission, cover, route, anchor availability, and edge composition (for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose. 11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier

(for example, avoiding those with loose or jagged rocks). The anchor selected should leave no doubt that it will work for its intended purpose. 11-62. Rappel ropes anchored at waist level or above make transitioning over the edge much easier and reduce the likelihood of Soldiers stumbling or falling. Stumbles and falls are likely to increase the risk of rope damage on sharp rock as well as increase force exerted on anchors. 11-63. Rappel sites with suitable loading and off-loading platforms should be selected. Ideally, they are flat and allow for anchoring far enough away from the edge that Soldiers do not need to be attached to an anchor to prevent accidentally falling off the edge. If this is impossible, use fixed-rope techniques described in section I when approaching the rappel point. A staging area large enough to hold the group in a safe place nearby is also desirable. INSTALLATION CONSIDERATIONS 11-64. The two major factors in deciding how to attach a rappel rope to an anchor are whether the rope needs to be retrievable from the bottom and whether redundancy in rappel rope strands is necessary for safety. Both characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time. 11-65. In

attach a rappel rope to an anchor are whether the rope needs to be retrievable from the bottom and whether redundancy in rappel rope strands is necessary for safety. Both characteristics cannot be achieved at the same time. 11-65. In an operational environment, or during advanced military mountaineering training, ropes must be retrievable. This is because there is presumably no other feasible way to negotiate the vertical obstacle, or the group would be using it. All people and equipment must rappel, and the rope must be recovered for future use. This means that the rope cannot be fixed to the top anchor when the last Soldier begins rappelling. 11-66. When training basic rappelling, retrieving ropes is not necessary. Appropriate rappel sites for inexperienced rappellers should include access between the top and bottom by some other safe means for set up and breakdown. This allows for a greater safety margin by using two fixed independent strands for rappel ropes. Not only does this add redundancy to the system, but also using two strands replicates typical rappelling in an operational environment. 11-67. Anchors that support the maximum force rappellers could exert should be established as described in chapter 9. All rigging should

does this add redundancy to the system, but also using two strands replicates typical rappelling in an operational environment. 11-67. Anchors that support the maximum force rappellers could exert should be established as described in chapter 9. All rigging should be inspected by a qualified advanced military mountaineer, at a minimum. RETRIEVABLE RAPPELS 11-68. Retrievable rappels can be established using appropriate single-point anchors (such as a tree, boulder, horn of rock) using only the rope, or they can be attached to cordelettes, or webbing tied around the anchor feature. If other materials are used, then they cannot be retrieved from the bottom. 11-69. Multipoint anchors require additional materials to establish. This material cannot be retrieved from the bottom. 11-70. The minimum necessary equipment should be used in building retrievable rappel anchors. 288 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Fixed Ropes Half-Rope Length 11-71. The simplest and most common method is to just run one end of the rope around anchor feature, and then double back stack it until the middle of the rope is around the anchor feature. This ensures both strands are the same length. Tie a stopper knot at the bottom end with both strands leaving 12- to 18-inch tails. This prevents accidentally rappelling off the end of the rope. The ropes are then thrown or back stacked over the edge. 11-72. Sometimes the rope cannot be routed directly around the anchor. The rope can then be back stacked so that the middle of the rope passes through the attachment point for an anchor made from cordelette or webbing or clipped to it using a locking carabiner. 11-73. If a rope could be cut, it is possible to make the system redundant for all but the last rappeller. Chapter 12 Hauling and Lowering Techniques Mountain warfare requires moving Soldiers, weapons, and equipment up, over, and down steep, rugged terrain. It is vital that Soldiers understand the principles and fundamental concepts of hauling and lowering heavy loads both efficiently and safely. SECTION I - HAULING TECHNIQUES 12-1. Mountain operations involve many situations that require hauling systems. A hauling system is a technical rope system used to move a load up steep or vertical terrain comprised of rigging that generates increased mechanical advantage (MA) and captures progress. Properly using hauling systems allows Soldiers to move heavy loads through terrain obstacles that would have been impossible to overcome otherwise. Common situations requiring these systems are equipment recovery, resupply, and rescue operations. Choosing the right system for a given situation requires understanding the principles of MA, categories of systems, and solid judgement. MECHANICAL ADVANTAGE 12-2. A mechanical advantage is a reduction in the force required to move a load, which comes at the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques. The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary

the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. During hauling operations, MA can be created using a rope through several rigging techniques. The advantage gained reduces the amount of force that is necessary to move a load vertically. This makes hauling heavy loads easier. When choosing and constructing a hauling system, the goal is to use the lowest level of MA to move the load. As MA increases, efficiency and load sensitivity decrease. Efficiency is lost throughout the system anytime the rope touches a surface (including the edge of the cliff), moves through carabiners or pulleys, and rubs on itself in the system. Load sensitivity is the ability of the Soldier pulling on the rope to feel what is happening to the load on the end of the rope. For example, a Soldier pulling a heavy load up a slope by hand will know immediately if the load becomes stuck on an obstacle. However, a Soldier moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time,

However, a Soldier moving the load using a high level of MA would not feel this until there was a large amount of tension in the system. This is important when moving casualties or sensitive equipment. These systems require time, materials, and personnel to construct and operate. The intent is not to make easy work of moving the load. The lowest level of MA is desired to maximize load sensitivity, efficiency, and time. 12-3. The more MA a rope system produces, the less efficient it will be. For example, a Soldier operating a 5:1 system only needs to exert 1/5 of the pulling force to move the load. However, that Soldier will need to pull 5 feet of rope through the system for the load to move 1 foot. A balance between work and efficiency must be achieved when selecting an appropriate MA for a given situation. HAULING SYSTEM COMPONENTS 12-4. The hauling system has five basic components. Understanding how they work to move the load together (see the list below) allows Soldiers to achieve greater efficiency during hauling: * Anchors-the anchors required for hauling a heavy load must be unquestionable (see chapter 9). Anchors should be located away from

TECHNIQUES TO REDUCE FRICTION 12-13. Friction reduces efficiency of rope movement and can drastically reduce MA. It is important to identify points of friction within the system and strive to reduce them. Efficiency is lost throughout the system anytime the rope touches hardware. Friction can be minimized by using pulleys. Pulleys are used to change direction in rope systems. Pulleys should be small, lightweight, and rated for mountaineering applications. They should accommodate the largest diameter of rope being used. Pulleys are made with several bearings, different-sized sheaves (wheels), and metal alloy side plates. (See figure 12-8, page 310.) Always avoid plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than

Always avoid plastic pulleys. The side plate should rotate on the pulley axle to allow the pulley to be attached at any point along the rope. For best results, the sheave diameter must be at least four times larger than the rope's diameter to maintain high rope strength. Pulleys with side plates designed to accommodate prusik knots are referred to as prusik minding pulleys. These pulleys are designed with tolerances that allow the ropes to run through them but block the passage of a prusik hitch, preventing it from being caught in the pulley. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 309

Chapter 12 Figure 12-8. Types of pulleys 12-14. Pulleys are estimated to be approximately 90-percent efficient, while carabiners are considered only 60-percent efficient. The difference between a system that uses pulleys at direction changes and the same system that only uses carabiners is significant. If the team only has a few pulleys, they should be used at the direction changes closest to the system's haul strand. Pulleys in these locations will maximize the force put into the system initially and carry 90-percent efficiency farther through the system. 12-15. Friction also occurs where the mainline contacts the edge of the slope or cliff. If a suitable anchor can be found near the edge, this friction point can be minimized. The mainline can be lifted and routed through a high directional at the top of the slope or cliff to reduce rope contact and friction at the edge. (See figure 12-9.) 310 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

This system is more of a permanent installation and is most often used on a main supply line. The description below is generalized and based on concepts. A lowering system is a technical rope system used to move a load down steep or vertical terrain in a controlled fashion using friction hitches or mechanical devices. These sorts of systems are used to control the speed of descent for personnel or equipment using rope. They are an integral part of both highand low-angle rescue. (See chapter 15.) Lowering a victim or a load is always preferred over hauling if the terrain and situation allows. No two situations are identical. Each new situation will dictate which lowering techniques and systems are appropriate. Understanding basic lowering concepts is key to achieving a safe and efficient solution to the problem. LOWERING CONCEPTS 12-23. There are many devices and techniques available depending on the weight of the load. The bottom line for any lowering system is that enough friction must be created to safely control the descent of the load. Different terrain demands different methods of creating friction. When the terrain is steep and broken, selecting a device or technique that provides varying levels of friction is preferred. 12-24. All lowering systems should be closed by securing the free end of the

Chapter 13 Mountain Stream Crossing In 480 BC, Persian King Xerxes constructed a pontoon bridge that spanned a mile and a quarter across the Hellespont. After a previous failure to take Greece, the king weighed the options of either finding alternate routes to the north that added months to his expedition or pinpoint potential water crossing locations for his army. Xerxes insisted on the fastest and most direct route across the Aegean inlet for his 300,000 men. While negotiating the linear obstacle involved massive resources and engineering, it would save precious time for his army to reach their objective. SECTION I - MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS 13-1. A mountain stream crossing is essentially an approach to negotiating a potentially swift and cold waterway that Soldiers may encounter in the mountains. Learning to cross small streams forms a foundation of skills for personnel to manage larger streams and rivers, where consequences could be far more hazardous. 13-2. In an operation involving the crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation

crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation should be conducted economically and with minimal loss of momentum. 13-3. There are limits on the safe use of the techniques discussed in this chapter. Not all mountain rivers or streams will be fordable with these techniques. If a water obstacle is too wide, swift, or deep, an alternate route should be used. It may require using aircraft transport if engineer support is unavailable. Reconnaissance of questionable crossing sites is essential. This chapter covers the techniques for crossing mountain streams that have a depth generally not exceeding waist level. 13-4. Stream crossings should not be taken lightly. The force of flowing water may be extremely great and is most often underestimated. All rivers and streams are obstacles to movement. They should be treated as danger areas and avoided whenever possible. When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed of the current,

should be treated as danger areas and avoided whenever possible. When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed of the current, and depth of the water. This activity should be rehearsed prior to execution in the operational environment. RECONNAISSANCE 13-5. Performing a site survey of potential crossing locations (map, photo, or aerial) may not always reveal that a water obstacle exists. In a swamp, for example, unfordable sloughs may not show on the map, and they may be concealed from aerial observation by a canopy of vegetation. 13-6. Site selection is extremely important once Soldiers determine that they must make a crossing. Elevated positions offer an optimal vantage point from which to analyze a large area of possibilities. This is sometimes better than a hundred close views from a riverbank. Select the site selection before the main body arrives and examine the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted. 13-7. A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or

the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted. 13-7. A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or swimming with ropes, and minimize drowning hazards. Care must be taken to avoid an installation team crossing upstream of rapids, waterfalls, or fallen trees in the river. For dry features, such as gorges or ravines, the site should facilitate the installation team's descent and ascent crossing while minimizing any falling hazards that exist. While dry crossings are preferred to wet crossings for speed and safety factors, they can become locations for an enemy to place landmines and improvised explosive devices. 13-8. The time of day is an important factor. Recent precipitation or increased temperatures could cause water levels to rise as glaciers or snow-covered peaks begin to melt. Early morning crossings are preferred, as the cooler night temperatures usually reduce the melt from snow and ice. A morning crossing also allows clothing items to dry throughout the day. Whether a crossing is made in daylight or in darkness depends on 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 323

Chapter 13 the need for concealment, proficiency of troops, nature of the terrain, characteristics of the water obstacle, enemy disposition and capabilities (such as minefields on far banks), and the need for speed. 13-9. A crossing point should be chosen where the river widens. The sudden width of the channel normally yields a shallow depth. Avoid sharp turns in the river or a narrowing choke point in the river or stream since the water is likely to be deep and have a strong current on the outside of the bend for curves. 13-10. Many mountain streams, especially those fed by glacier runoff, contain sections with numerous braided channels. While often shallower than a main river, this changing landscape offers little in the way of cover and concealment of exposed personnel. Shoals, or partially submerged sandbars, can act like quicksand depending on the riverbed composition. 13-11. Riverbanks should be low enough to accommodate for easy entry and exit from the water. Banks that are tall and steep may require employing installations such as hasty rappels (see figure 11-11, page 293) or simple fixed ropes (see figure 11-2, page 278). 13-12. Logjams and other large obstructions present their own hazards. Floating debris,

Banks that are tall and steep may require employing installations such as hasty rappels (see figure 11-11, page 293) or simple fixed ropes (see figure 11-2, page 278). 13-12. Logjams and other large obstructions present their own hazards. Floating debris, while often hung up in shallow spots, can potentially hit personnel in the water. Water flowing around logjams creates riverbed erosion and swift waters. If crossing upstream of logjams, ensure that Soldiers are far enough away to react and do not become entangled in branches beneath the water surface. 13-13. When possible, cross with ample overwatch in place for support and with an approach that offers minimal detection by enemy forces. PREPARATION OF TROOPS AND EQUIPMENT 13-14. Most of the preparation should happen long before entering the water, with only special considerations executed in a short halt prior. Preparation should include- * Water-sensitive items. Chapter 14 Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Ten percent of the Earth's land mass is covered by glaciers. Glaciers are rivers of ice flowing under the influence of gravity, constantly restructuring the mountains around them. They often provide the best route in otherwise impassable terrain but can contain crevasses and other hazards that can cause injury, death, or compromise a unit's mission. Soldiers operating in glaciated terrain must understand these hazards, be well versed in the fundamentals of glacier travel, and be proficient with crevasse rescue techniques. SECTION I - GLACIER FUNDAMENTALS 14-1. Glaciers can be large enough to cover an entire continent. They may move only inches or hundreds of feet a year. Movement is caused by gravity, slippage over the bedrock, or by the internal flow in the ice. It is important for route planning and risk management to understand glacial features and understand how they form and move. Dismounted movement across glaciers is hazardous; however, glaciers often provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. GLACIERS 14-2. Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the

provide the easiest passage through more technical terrain on surrounding slopes and faces. GLACIERS 14-2. Glaciers form over time by the weight of accumulating snow compressing older layers of snow into ice. As snow accumulates, gravity takes over and the ice begins to move downhill. The weight of millions of pounds of ice makes a small film of water that acts as a lubricant, enabling it to slide. 14-3. The upper part of the glacier where the annual snow accumulation exceeds the melt is called the accumulation zone. Further down the glacier, the area where melt exceeds accumulation is an area called the ablation zone. The imaginary line between the two zones is known as the firn line. CLASSIFICATION 14-4. There are two classifications of glaciers: alpine glaciers and ice caps. Alpine glaciers form in high mountain bowls. Ice caps can cover thousands of square miles, such as those that cover Greenland and Antarctica. TYPES OF ALPINE GLACIERS 14-5. The following are four types of glaciers: * Valley glacier-resides and flows in a valley. * Cirque glacier-forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl. * Hanging glacier-these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers

following are four types of glaciers: * Valley glacier-resides and flows in a valley. * Cirque glacier-forms and resides in a bowl. These do not advance beyond the bowl. * Hanging glacier-these are a result of valley or cirque glaciers flowing and deteriorating. As the movement continues, portions separate and are sometimes left hanging on mountains, ridgelines, or cliffs. * Piedmont glacier-formed by one or more valley glaciers, spreads out into a large area. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 333

Chapter 14 GLACIER OBSTACLES 14-6. Units intending to use glaciers for travel routes must be familiar with their hazards and characteristics to ensure safe and efficient movement on them. Failure to identify and prepare for obstacles, which can come in the form of vertical terrain, can slow or prevent movement. Failure to identify and prepare for hazards can result in significant injury or loss of life. 14-7. Glaciers contain many different features that can impede travel. (See figure 14-1.) They are- * Bergschrund-the bergschrund is a giant crevasse found at the upper limit of glacier movement. It is formed where the moving glacier breaks away from the ice cap or snowfield above. The bergschrund can be high and overhanging and can create an obstacle to movement when moving from the valley floor onto the mountainsides. * Crevasses-crevasses are cracks in the glacier caused by irregularities in the bedrock under the glacier as it moves and flows. Crevasses often form where the angle of the slope increases greatly, causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction

the angle of the slope increases greatly, causing tension to split open the snow and ice. They also commonly form wherever the glacier makes a turn. They can be transverse, longitudinal, or lateral, depending on their orientation to the direction of the glacier's movement. Crevasses can be 200-feet deep but are normally 40- to 100-feet deep. Crevasses often hinder travel across glaciers. Snow often conceals crevasses, causing possible major falling hazards to Soldiers. Bypassing them can increase travel time and distance. Snow bridges that form over them can give way without warning. During the summer, the ice is less covered with snow and most crevasses are exposed. They can still be hazardous at night or in reduced visibility. * Moat-the moat is a gap formed where the snow and ice are melted by the warmer rock along the edge of a glacier. The edge of a moat is often undercut. Depending on its size, the moat may be an obstacle to moving on or off the glacier. * Icefalls-icefalls result from the flow of the glacier down a steep ridge. The ridge forces the ice up into a jumbled mass as the glacier flows over the rock. These present formidable
