These present formidable obstacles and should be avoided. * Serac-seracs are ice walls and towers that form in icefalls or on the lower edge of hanging glaciers. They are unstable and can fall unexpectedly. Travel below seracs or hanging glaciers should be avoided when possible. * Nunatak-a nunatak is an island of bedrock that protrudes up through the glacier, creating an obstacle to glacial movement. It creates pressure in the ice that can form crevasses, seracs, and icefalls. * Water hazards-streams that run on the surface and then disappear into a hole are called moulins. Moulins form when meltwater from the glacier finds a crevasse and moves to the ground below the ice. A fall into a moulin can carry a Soldier into the glacier and result in almost certain drowning. Chapter 14 ICE AXE AND CRAMPONS 14-12. Ice axes and crampons may be necessary for movement over snow or ice on a glacier but also provide the ability for a Soldier on a rope team to self-arrest to control, stop, and hold the fall of another climber. Ice axes may also be used for snow anchor construction for crevasse rescue. SKIS AND SNOWSHOES 14-13. In deep snow conditions, skis or snowshoes make movement more efficient. They also distribute weight over a greater area when crossing crevasses, which can reduce the likelihood of breaking through a hidden snow bridge. Snowshoes may be more practical than skis for roped glacier travel unless all members of a rope team are skilled skiers. PRUSIKS, SLINGS, AND CORDELETTES 14-14. Short prusik loops, slings, and cordelettes can be used for ascending a rope after a crevasse fall. They are used for belaying rope team members and creating anchors, load transfers, and hauling systems in crevasse rescue. Slings can be used to improvise a chest harness, if necessary, and can be useful to rig the rucksack for removal in the event of a fall. Each Soldier should carry a cordelette, a sling, and a short prusik. SNOW

Each Soldier should carry a cordelette, a sling, and a short prusik. SNOW ANCHORS 14-15. Snow or ice anchors, such as pickets and ice screws, are often carried for use in crevasse rescue. In some snow conditions, ice axes, skis, and other items may be used to create an anchor. WANDS 14-16. Wands are sticks used as markers and can be utilized in many ways. They can be used to mark the location of known crevasses on frequently used routes or used in pairs forming an X to indicate danger. They can be used while setting up bivouac sites to mark the boundaries of safe areas. They are sometimes useful for whiteout navigation in heavily crevassed terrain. Wands can be made using 4-foot bamboo garden stakes with tape or flagging. OTHER GLACIAL GEAR 14-17. USE OF THE ROPE 14-18. A central question when considering travel over glaciers is whether to use a rope for fall protection. The hazard of hidden crevasses on a glacier varies considerably. In some circumstances, it may be preferable to travel unroped on crevassed glaciers; however, this is not typical. Deciding whether to rope together as a team depends upon the season, mode of travel, snow conditions, and the conditions of the glacier itself. 14-19. Traveling unroped is faster. It makes communication and dissemination of information easier; it can be done with untrained Soldiers. It eliminates the transition times required for tying in and preparing for roped travel. HAZARD VERSUS CREVASSE HAZARD 14-21. In glaciated terrain, there can be both a risk of falling on steep ground as well as a risk of falling into crevasses. These risks are not managed in the same way. Crevasse hazard is best managed with good route finding and by keeping 8 to 10 meters of rope between Soldiers. Rope teams can usually stop crevasse falls because these occur on low-angled terrain without falling hazard. On flat terrain or soft snow, the arresting Soldiers are not typically at risk of sliding into the crevasse and are often able to stop the fall by slumping in the snow, rather than a full team self-arrest. 14-22. It should not have unnecessary slack or be taut. Excess slack will cause a Soldier to fall deeper into a crevasse, placing more force on other members of the team and increasing the difficulty of arresting the fall. The falling climber is more likely to hit something or become stuck or wedged. 14-34. A rope with the correct amount of tension lies on the snow with a gentle curve, out of the way of the feet. It can be helpful to hold the rope to the front when traveling downhill and to the rear when traveling uphill. Pace should be adjusted to maintain correct tension in the rope by feel, especially during stops and starts. During sharp turns, the rope tends to go slack as the lead Soldier makes a change in the direction of travel, but then it becomes taut as the next Soldier approaches the turn. Chapter 14 ROUTE FINDING AND CREVASSE DETECTIONS 14-37. Crevasse falls are extremely dangerous, even when traveling roped up with experienced Soldiers. Even when all Soldiers manage the rope well and the fall is stopped immediately, severe injuries can result. Ice axes, crampons, and collapsing snow bridges can cause injuries. Detection and avoidance are the primary skills needed to eliminate the need for crevasse rescue. On heavily crevassed glaciers, it is advisable to use an advanced party to scout and mark the safest route in advance of the main body. This can save hours of wandering, slow progress, and running into dead ends. Once relatively safe routes are established, it can reduce the skill and experience level required of the main body. INFORMATION GATHERING 14-38. Big picture views of the terrain can be very helpful. A maze of crevasses can be analyzed more easily from above than from within. It is a good idea to take digital photos whenever high ground provides a vantage point. Because glaciers move so slowly, crevasse patterns remain constant from year to year, making even old photographs useful for study. Intelligence products or online mapping resources (see appendix B) that contain satellite imagery can provide overhead

Intelligence products or online mapping resources (see appendix B) that contain satellite imagery can provide overhead views. These may contain imagery taken during the summer or late season and show the general trends and locations of dense crevasses that may be only partially filled in or have suspect snow bridges when traveling during winter and early season. TIMING 14-39. On snow covered and heavily crevassed glaciers, snow bridges are firmer at night or early in the morning. If stable, they can often provide more direct lines of travel. Warmer daytime temperatures can soften these snow bridges, increasing the likelihood of crevasse fall. This may require finding a longer alternative route. 14-40. Be cautious after snowstorms. Fresh snow can fill in and blend in what might otherwise be detectable crevasses. 14-41. Seasonal timing is equally important. Although unit leaders may not have much say in the time of year they are required to travel on glaciers, a basic understanding of how seasonal changes affect surface conditions is important. Below are descriptions of typical conditions in the midlatitudes: * Autumn-in late season conditions, most crevasses are clearly visible and snow bridges have melted out to their maximum extent. Travel is generally safest, as there is little risk of unexpected crevasse fall, but route finding can be difficult and require long detours and lengthy movement times around crevasse fields. In steeper terrain, firm conditions can make falling hazard a higher concern. * Winter-early winter is especially hazardous. Unconsolidated snow hides crevasses but often does not effectively bridge them. Crevasses are more difficult to detect, and unexpected falls are more likely. In late winter, deeper snow conditions may provide more effective snow bridges. Increased snow loads may cause bridges to sag, making detection easier. Skis or snowshoes are often required. * Spring-snowfall has reached its maximum depth, making glacier travel safest. * Spring-snowfall has reached its maximum depth, making glacier travel safest. Snow bridges are at their strongest and the snowpack strengthens from warmer weather. Skis or snowshoes are often required, but lines of travel are typically much more direct. * Summer-early morning travel on firm snow surfaces makes travel easier, but snow bridges are beginning to weaken. Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue ZONES OF TENSION AND COMPRESSION 14-43. Crevasses are formed by tension. Tension is created as glacier ice stretches over rolls in the terrain and where it stretches due to different rates of flow within the glacier. These crevasses form perpendicular to the direction of the stretch. Recognizing where this tension is likely to occur can help with predicting their likely locations when snow fills in or conceals them. Crevasses are more likely at the top of a roll, where the terrain gets steeper and drops away below it. They are also common near the edges of valley glaciers, where additional drag and friction occurs against the valley walls, and the center of the glacier is moving faster. These "marginal" crevasses point toward the center of the glacier at an angle. For this same reason, the centers of glaciers generally have fewer crevasses and are preferred travel routes. 14-44. Compression zones occur where the underlying bedrock flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of

flattens out and where glacial ice slows down or piles up. Here, crevasses become narrow and eventually disappear. Glacial ice can also pile up in bowls and flat benches in the terrain and where glaciers flow together. These areas of compression can be relatively crevasse-free. Observing these zones and working to link them together are keys to good route finding. SURFACE CLUES 14-45. Clues to locating crevasses below the surface of the snow can be subtle and difficult to recognize, but it is important for determining an appropriate crossing technique. It can also be just as important to recognize similar clues that do not indicate crevasses and to not waste time and effort on long detours. * Sagging-snow covering larger crevasses gradually deforms and sags under its own weight. Early in the process, this may be barely noticeable, but later the outlines of the crevasse become more defined. Sometimes a slight change in sheen or texture can be observed. Other times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change

times, a slight change in color, from dust or windblown snow settling in a subtle depression, can be visible. These should be approached with caution. Snow is, however, an inherently uneven surface, so not every dip, groove, or color change represents a crevasse. In low visibility or flat light, these can be impossible to recognize. * Nearby crevasses-since crevasses are often found in groups and tend to form parallel to one another, look for other crevasses, patterns, or depressions nearby that have similar orientation. * Parallel cracks-in the case of larger crevasses, parallel thin cracks can sometimes form at the edges of a giant snow bridge. Although these can have the appearance of two narrow crevasses, they can be the boundaries of a single, giant snow bridge. PROBING 14-46. Snow probing in areas that look suspicious can be done using an ice axe. It can identify crevasses, determine its true lip, and investigate the extent, length, and width of a crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a

crevasse. To probe, the shaft of the axe is thrust into the snow a couple feet ahead of where one moves, looking for a noticeable reduction in resistance. If there is a sudden drop in resistance, there is likely a crevasse, but it can also be a soft snow layer. Probing requires experience to accurately interpret. The short length of an ice axe makes this difficult. Avalanche probes and ski poles with the basket removed are better choices, if available. Probing is also required for determining safe bivouac locations. CROSSING TECHNIQUES 14-47. There are a variety of options and techniques for crossing crevasses, and leaders must understand and be capable of incorporating any combination of them to adapt to the terrain. Rope teams should travel perpendicular to the direction of crevasses to reduce the risk of exposing more than one Soldier at a time. (See figure 14-6, page 344.) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 343

Sometimes it is preferable to cross at one end of a crevasse where its width narrows, rather than take a chance with a snow bridge. (See figure 14-7.) With large crevasses, this could lead to traveling a quarter of a mile or more to gain 30 feet of forward progress. In winter or spring, seasonal snow may still cover the narrow ends of a crevasse. What looks like the end of the crevasse might not be its actual end. This assessment can require some judgement. Chapter 14 Jumping 14-50. Only conduct jumping when the gap is short. Running leaps requiring big push offs from suspect crevasse lips and falls can result in serious injury. Jumping should not be attempted unless there are no other options. Enough slack must be provided for the jumper to clear the crevasse without question. Be wary of catching a crampon and use common sense. Climbing into the Crevasse 14-51. Occasionally, it may be practical to climb down into a shallow crevasse and climb back out the other side. Standard belay techniques (see chapter 10) should be used. Be especially aware of bottoms that appear solid but are not. Echelon Formation 14-52. This keeps team members still to the rear but offset slightly to the side. This provides an alternative to following the leader's tracks in a single-file line. This should only be used on heavily crevassed sections where all crevasses are visible and there is very little risk of falling into a hidden one. Figure 14-9. Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue CREVASSE FALL CONSIDERATIONS 14-54. Mutually supporting rope teams should have a minimum of one Soldier per team who is trained in crevasse rescue. This will ensure that rescue capability can always be provided, even when the more experienced member of another rope team is the one to fall in. Two trained Soldiers are necessary in rope teams traveling independently, away from supporting teams. 14-55. Crevasse falls are rarely dramatic and sudden falls that rip team members off their feet and result in someone dangling down inside an abyss. In fact, most crevasse falls involve breaking through a snow bridge but falling no further than waste deep, and with minimal force exerted on team members. Despite this, Soldiers must be trained to deal with more severe falls and be able to adapt and adjust to a variety of circumstances. Options for crevasse rescue involve an abundance of variables. They depend largely upon the breakdown of rope teams, the number of Soldiers per rope, conditions of the glacier, and specific equipment carried. The following steps should be considered in the event of a crevasse fall with a three-person rope team. STOP THE FALL 14-57. Stop the fall immediately. Some falls may be barely noticeable, while others may require dropping into the self-arrest position in the opposite direction. Stopping falls on firm surfaces can be more difficult than soft ones. Once the fall is arrested, both rescuers should kick crampon points into the snow to establish a strong, stable position to prevent the victim from slipping any further. Communication can often be made with the victim at this point. In circumstances where Soldiers have only fallen a few feet or are stuck in the snow bridge, they may be able to climb out unassisted. Chapter 14 Figure 14-10. Stopping a crevasse fall CONSTRUCT AN ANCHOR AND TRANSFER THE LOAD 14-58. When another rope team is available, then they can construct an anchor and help the team transfer the load of the fallen Soldier onto it. (See figure 14-11.) Otherwise, the Soldier on the opposite end is usually the one to complete this step. End Soldiers slowly get out of the self-arrest, making sure that middle Soldiers can still hold the weight. End Soldiers establish an anchor (see chapter 9 for snow and ice anchors) below the middle climber and towards the crevasse. They attach a prusik to the loaded rope and clip it to the anchor with a locking carabiner. If there is limited distance between the middle climber and the crevasse lip, the anchor can be constructed above the middle climber. Once pressure is relieved from middle Soldiers, it is common for them to continue backing up this anchor while the end climber improves it or constructs additional components. This anchor must be unquestionably strong, as it may be used to haul the Soldier out. The prusik should also be backed up with a suitable knot clipped to the anchor. Figure 14-11. To make a clear assessment and develop a plan, it is best to approach the edge of the crevasse where the fallen Soldier can be seen and heard. This can be done by one of the team members using a safety prusik attached to the unweighted portion of the rope. Exercise caution approaching the edge. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. Determination of what to do next will depend on how far down the climbers are, whether they sustained injuries, extent of any injuries, and characteristics of the terrain in and around the crevasse. The loaded rope can often become entrenched into the lip of the crevasse, complicating rescue options. This may be a good time to pad underneath the rope to prevent this from becoming worse with an ice axe shaft, foam pad, or rucksack slid underneath the rope as close to the edge as can be reached. This can take some work, and items used for padding should be anchored so that it cannot fall into the crevasse. Various options for rescue are described below. Self-Rescue 14-61. Self-rescue can be achieved by the fallen climber ascending the rope itself using a prusik ascent (see paragraphs 11-39 through 11-49, pages 282 through 284) or other techniques discussed in chapter 11 and is also shown in figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. figure 14-10, page 348. When possible, this is often the easiest and fastest option. The prusik ascent prevents the fallen Soldier from becoming cold waiting for rescuers. Getting the weight of the rucksack off the body and onto the rope is also particularly helpful for staying upright. Assistance from team members may be required to surmount the crevasse lip. The method does not work if the fallen Soldier sustained significant injuries. Belay 14-62. Belays may be a fast, easy option when crampons and ice axes can be used to climb out of the hole, especially if or when the rope is too entrenched in the crevasse lip to prusik out. The remaining free end of the rope can be passed down to the fallen climber to tie into the harness with, while a team member above creates a belay at the anchor. Chapter 14 Haul 14-63. If none of the above options are viable, a more complex solution of hauling the fallen climber out will be needed. HAULING 14-64. Hauling techniques used for MA described in chapter 12 may be used for hauling; however, there are circumstances specific to working with crevasses that must be considered. Direct Haul 14-65. This refers to hauling systems constructed on the fallen climber's weighted strand of rope. A common example is the 3:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-4, page 307.) This is constructed by untying the backup knot behind the prusik and using this remaining rope to construct the system. A disadvantage to the direct haul is that it does not work if the rope is entrenched in the crevasse lip. This method is also impractical if there are knots tied in the weighted rope to help hold the crevasse fall. (See figure 14-12.) Figure 14-12. Glacier Travel and Crevasse Rescue Drop Loop 14-66. Drop loops refer to hauling systems that use a bight of rope sent down and attach to the fallen climber's harness, independent of the climber's weighted strand. (See figure 14-13.) An example is the 2:1 hauling system. (See figure 12-3, page 307.) This is often the preferred method because the crevasse lip can be padded prior to hauling and because the victim can often assist by pulling on the strand opposite the haul strand. Drop-loop hauls do require victims to clip the bight of rope into the harness, so in the case of an unconscious victim, this step may need to be done by first rappelling to them then re-ascending. Drop-loop systems can be performed using the remainder of the rope or by a separate rope team utilizing a different rope altogether. Progress must still be captured during the haul for safety. This may be done by pulling rope through the prusik on the original tensioned rope. Figure 14-13. Drop-loop rescue system (2:1) 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 351

Chapter 15 Mountain Rescue and Evacuation A unit's capability to conduct mountain rescue and evacuation is a critical part of mountain operations. Swift and efficient rescue can mean the difference between success and failure of a mission or even the survival of a casualty. In mountainous terrain, even relatively minor injuries may require evacuation. The type of injury, distance to be moved, terrain, training level of the team, and litter capabilities determine the evacuation technique chosen. Air evacuation is preferred. However, the weather, tactical situation, or operational ceiling of the aircraft may make this impossible. Therefore, it is imperative that all personnel are trained in mountain evacuation techniques and are self-sufficient. Casualties should be triaged before evacuation. The most experienced medical personnel available perform triage (physician, physician's assistant, or medic). SECTION I - RESCUE OPERATIONS 15-1. Every commander should have a MEDEVAC plan before undertaking an operation. This plan should have dedicated assets (primary, alternate, contingency, and emergency) in place so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting

so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting winds reduce the ability of fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft to assist in operations. Therefore, relying solely on aircraft or specialized equipment is a poor substitute for careful planning. 15-2. The two types of rescue operations encountered by units operating in mountainous environments are deliberate and improvised. DELIBERATE 15-3. Deliberate rescue is when the mission objective itself is a rescue operation, thus allowing time for focused planning and the use of specialized rescue specific equipment. IMPROVISED 15-4. Improvised rescue situations are encountered when a casualty is sustained during normal operations and conducting a rescue was not the intended objective. Even improvised rescue operations should be practiced and rehearsed to minimize the negative effects on mission capability. All operations should have a CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a

CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a potential rescue. PLANNING 15-5. The rescue tasks must be identified by obtaining the following information: * Number of casualties by precedence (urgent, priority, routine, convenience). * Number of casualties by type (litter or ambulatory) and the nature of their injuries. * Terrain features and with respect to the location of the casualties. * Tactical situation. * Any assets available to aid in security, rescue, treatment, and evacuation. * If treatment can be provided at the scene or if the casualty requires movement to a safer location. * Additional personnel or equipment required for the rescue operation. * Any circumstances that may require specialized skills. * Weather conditions. * Difficulty of the terrain. * Time available. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 353

Chapter 15 15-6. Route selection when planning mountain CASEVAC often depends upon technical capabilities. In some cases, trained personnel and equipment available for low- or high-angle rescue may allow for safer, less physically demanding operations. A lack of these resources and capabilities may require traveling longer distances around steeper terrain, greatly increasing the burden on rescuers. CONSIDERATIONS 15-7. Time considerations can cause a leader to compromise planning stages or treatment (beyond first aid). Make a realistic estimate of time available as quickly as possible to determine the action time remaining. The key elements are the casualty's condition and ability to endure the environment. Time available is a balance between these conditions and the resources and personnel available. 15-8. There are many additional considerations for the rescue team during deliberate rescue: * Typically, team members must distribute and carry all equipment, including hot food and drinks, stoves, sleeping bags, bivouac equipment, warm clothes, ropes, and stretchers. * Evacuation routes often require extensive preparation and can involve establishing anchor points, belays, fixed ropes, lowers, and raises. * Altitude and visibility can greatly affect the team as well as the casualty. Maximum use of secure, reliable trails or roads is essential. * Protection

Maximum use of secure, reliable trails or roads is essential. * Protection from the elements, such as blankets, tarps, warming layers and rain gear, can be vital. Even a mild rain can complicate an otherwise simple rescue. In higher altitudes, extreme cold or strong winds can greatly increase the rescue's time and complexity. GENERAL STEPS 15-9. Regardless of whether a rescue is deliberate or improvised, the following steps must be taken upon arrival at the rescue site to accomplish a safe and efficient rescue operation: * Assume command-one person and one person only is in charge. * Scene safety-prevent further injuries to the casualty and to others. Explore all options for casualty access prior to committing to one. Use reasonable care in reaching the casualty. Rescuers must not become casualties. * Immediately ensure the casualty has an open airway, control serious bleeding, and protect the casualty from further harm and from environmental hazards. If the casualty is unconscious, continually monitor for a pulse. * Do not move the casualty until determining the extent of injuries unless necessary to prevent further injury or if the casualty is in a dangerous or exposed location. * Do nothing more until the situation has been thoroughly considered. Resist the urge for action. Speed is less important than correct actions and decision making. The decisions made on scene drive the rest of the rescue (for example, casualty rigging, packaging, route selection, anchors, and rope systems). * Decide whether to evacuate with available resources or to send or call for help. Speed in getting to the next level of care must be balanced against the probability of further injury. This is especially crucial if working with inexperienced personnel, insufficient equipment, or terrain or weather hazards. * When the evacuation route is long and arduous, a series of litter relay points or stations should be established, if possible. These stations should be staffed with the medical personnel and equipment necessary to provide proper treatment. * Helicopters or heated vehicles, if available, should be used for evacuation. While the use of aircraft or vehicles is preferred and can expedite a rescue operation, evacuation of a seriously wounded Soldier should never be delayed awaiting aircraft, vehicle, or a change in weather. PROLONGED FIELD CARE 15-11. The mountain environment is defined by austere and remote conditions. This environment, combined with the difficulty of patient movement, creates situations that can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02). 15-12. Medical personnel with standard training

can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02). 15-12. Medical personnel with standard training may be required to perform beyond their skillset. Specific training should be conducted to prepare medical and nonmedical personnel for prolonged field care situations. Tactical combat casualty care uses protocols aimed primarily at preventing mortality in the first few hours of treatment, prior to arrival at surgical resuscitative care. However, patients in the mountains lacking fast and immediate evacuation are often at risk for complications, such as sepsis, multi-organ system failure, respiratory compromise, and other serious conditions. Prolonged field care begins with the sound principles of tactical combat casualty care, but when care is extended over hours or days, treatment must continuously be re-evaluated. Diligence is necessary to minimize the effect of potentially harmful interventions and to prevent, recognize, and treat conditions that may develop over time. 15-13. Critical patients ultimately require care in a hospital with surgery, blood products, an intensive care unit, and advanced imaging. This could be a result of sustaining relatively minor injuries, not having a litter available, or not having the available personnel for litter transport. Alternatively, these could involve moving a casualty in technical terrain that is not suited for transport in a litter. If casualties are able, they can walk, with one or more rescuers walking alongside, to provide physical support. A rescuer close behind can help in difficult terrain. Casualties can also be placed in a seat or improvised harness and lowered or hauled through steep terrain using the techniques described in chapter 12. The following litters are readily available to mountaineering units: * The poleless, nonrigid litter is lightweight and readily available but is the least favored litter. It does little to protect the patient's injuries and is not appropriate for attachment to any rope system. * The standard collapsible litter is readily available in all units and may be rigged for movement over rough mountainous terrain. However, it is not suitable for carry as a contingency litter due to its bulk and weight. * A rigid, metal-framed, basket-style litter that is rated for hoist operations is very well-suited for moving casualties through mountainous environments. These litters provide excellent patient protection and spinal immobilization, and when rigged properly, can readily attach to a variety of technical rope systems. The drawbacks to this type of litter are that it is heavy and is not designed to slide over surfaces. This is the preferred litter for mountain operations due to its versatility and relatively low weight. However, it is not a spinal immobilization device. The decisions made during initial packaging will affect the physical and mental outcomes for the casualty in the end. 15-27. For longer movements, it can be useful to add slings or cordelettes to the litter rim or handles for each litter bearer. In severely uneven terrain, such as talus or boulder fields, the pass-through technique can make movement safer for both the casualty and rescuers, provided extra personnel are available. To conduct the pass-through technique, simply have extra litter bearers take up static positions in the terrain ahead of the litter and as close to one another as possible. The litter is then passed forward into the hands of the extra litter bearers. As soon as litter bearers in the rear become obsolete, they move around and take up a new position further ahead in the direction of travel. They then wait until the litter reaches them and repeat the technique. This allows rescuers to remain still as the litter is transported, taking advantage of secure footing and stable positions. In this way, the litter is less likely to be dropped and litter bearers are less likely to sustain an injury attempting to move and carry the heavy load at the same time.

Low-angle rescue can generally be categorized by roped litter evacuations on low to moderately steep slopes where much of the weight of the casualty and rescuer is still supported by the ground. High-angle rescue generally refers to roped evacuations down steep cliffs and 5th-class terrain. High-angle rescue requires formal training, experience, excellent judgement, and good technical problem-solving skills. It often requires a substantial amount of time. Only level 2 and 3 military mountaineers should only conduct high-angle rescue, when necessary. There are often many variables involved in high-angle rescue, and thus, there is no prescriptive set way to deal with the many challenges that can be encountered. Because a combination of skills and techniques may ultimately be required, including climbing techniques, belays, rappels, hauling and lowering methods, or even the use of high lines, a comprehensive focus is well beyond the scope of this training circular. Rather, this section will focus on some of the fundamental principles and commonly used tools and techniques. LITTER RIGGING 15-48. Chapter 15 ROPE SELECTION 15-51. Rope rescue systems should meet the industry standard 10:1 static system safety factor (SSSF). Calculate the SSSF by first determining the force created by the rescue load. Each person attached to the system is estimated to create 1 kN. Therefore, one casualty and one rescuer are estimated to be a 2-kN load. For a 2-kN load, all components of the rescue system must be rated to 20-kN breaking strength to meet the 10:1 SSSF requirement. In this case, ropes would require a minimum breaking strength of around 30 kN to account for an estimated 1/3 strength loss when knots are tied into the rope. Most static kernmantle ropes 11 mm in diameter meet this 30 kN threshold. However, for mountain rescue operations, it is much more practical to use lighter weight ropes that can more easily be carried, allow for faster response times, and function better with other components of the mountaineering kits. These may have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of

have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of edge abrasion issues. These ropes should be static (low stretch) and should have a minimum diameter of 9.5 mm and a minimum breaking strength of 26 kN. 15-52. Rescues can be carried out using single or tandem rope systems. Single Rope 15-53. Single rope technique, much like that described for use with low-angle rescue, is typically simpler to construct and operate, and generally requires less equipment overall. However, it does not include redundancy for system or rope failure. Equipment breakage or human error can have catastrophic results. Consider using this technique only when there is no prominent edge transition, no sharp rock edges on the pitch, and time and resources are limited. Tandem Rope 15-54. Tandem rope technique is more complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct. However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult

complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct. However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult edge transitions due to the potential for high-peak forces in the event of failure, sharp rock edges, or when there is limited team experience regarding the rigging of anchors and lowering or belay systems. 15-55. Tandem rope technique uses two separate ropes referred to as the main line and the belay line. Each rope system requires a separate anchor. The main line is used to haul or lower the litter, and the belay line is there in case of main line failure. 15-56. The two ropes are connected to the litter attachment point with interlocking long tailed bowlines. (See figure 15-10.) The tail or free end of each bowline is used as a secondary attachment point for the patient and the litter attendant. 366 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Chapter 15 Figure 15-11. Tandem prusik belay LOWERING 15-58. Sites suitable for lowering should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential should be avoided when lowering is necessary. The litter and attendant can be lowered using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12, but techniques that generally provide greater friction are preferred. The end of the rope should be tied off to close the system. RAISING 15-59. Sites suitable for hauling should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential should be avoided when hauling is necessary. The litter and attendant may be hauled using techniques described in chapter 12. Systems with higher ratios may be necessary, as well as redirection and piggyback techniques. BELAY LINE 15-60. While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load will

While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load will be significant due to the short amount of rope available to absorb the force, and the static nature of all the system components. The separate belay line is also here for this purpose. If a high directional is used, the belay line should not be routed through it. This would cause a greater fall distance before the belay line could catch the load in the event of failure or breakage of the high directional. 15-61. While there are manufactured devices available that meet the criteria for a technical rescue belay, the simplest and most field expedient method is called the tandem prusik belay. Two prusiks, preferably made from 7- or 8-mm nylon static utility cord are tied approximately 2-inches apart on the belay line. The length of the prusik closer to the anchor should be a few inches shorter than the other prusik. These prusiks are then attached to the belay anchor with a locking carabiner. To use the belay,

Mountain Rescue and Evacuation together and the downhill hand on the downhill side of the rope. Feed rope through the prusiks with a "hitchhikers grip" (thumbs out) and keep a bow of rope approximately 8 to 12 inches of slack between the hands. There should be only a few inches of slack between the downhill hand and the litter. In the event of a blown edge transition or of main line failure, the prusiks will be ripped out of the belayer's hands and catch the load. The team leader has overall responsibility for the operation. The team leader considers all available options and selects the most appropriate technique for the situation. The team leader makes judgments based on the nature or urgency of the injury, the tactical situation, the nature of the terrain, and the personnel and resources available. Precise commands and singular control are necessary for safe operations. All commands should originate either with the team leader, control, or, in some cases, the edge safety. A variety of commands can be used but must be short, simple, and clear. Always include the name of the position in the command, such as SLACK ON MAIN or TENSION ON BELAY. Before any lowering or raising operations take place, a roll call is necessary to ensure all personnel are ready. Once all personnel are ready and checked and the litter and attendant are in position, begin the operation by calling UP ON MAIN or DOWN ON MAIN. Once the litter is moving, the speed can be adjusted, as necessary. To halt all movement, call STOP. All teams continue to act as if the load is on belay until the command OFF BELAY is given. 15-71. Chapter 16 Rope Bridges Operations in mountainous terrain often encounter obstacles, such as fast flowing water, ravines, or rock fields. Well-trained mountaineers can exploit this terrain with the use of rope bridges and high lines. These allow units to take the terrain out of the equation by using a rope suspended in the air to cross the obstacle. High lines are a type of rope bridge. The two terms are often used synonymously, and the techniques are relatively interchangeable; however, for the purposes of this training circular, we will refer to rope bridges when used for assisting personnel for river crossings and the term "high lines" to denote rope installations used to span longer or higher gaps in terrain. SECTION I - TECHNIQUES 16-1. A rope bridge is a rope tensioned between two anchors and suspended off the ground to assist units with crossing rivers. These are sometimes necessary in situations with swift and dangerous currents or very cold water, where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important. 16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are

where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important. 16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are fixed and potentially split by the river obstacle for prolonged periods. This can put them at a significant tactical disadvantage. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more VDA-crossing considerations.) CONSTRUCTION 16-3. The rope bridge is constructed using a static rope. The rope is anchored on the far side of the obstacle in the same manner as described for using handlines in paragraphs 13-26 through 13-29, page 327. It is then tensioned and anchored on the near side of the obstacle. A rope bridge may be built many ways depending upon the tactical situation and area to be crossed. However, all rope bridges share common safety principles for construction and use. Rope bridges must be tensioned as low as practical on the anchor while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation. METHODS OF TENSIONING 16-4. There are

while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation. METHODS OF TENSIONING 16-4. There are multiple ways to apply tension to a rope. The method selected depends on the length of the bridge, equipment available, personnel available, and time. Regardless of the method used, the principle remains the same; apply just enough tension to facilitate ease of crossing through the terrain. WARNING Ropes must not be overtensioned. An overtensioned rope is in its weakest state, and the system can apply exponential forces during use. Critical failures can occur with overtensioned ropes. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 371

Chapter 16 HAND TIGHT 16-5. The simplest and least equipment-intensive method is hand tightening the rope. Once Soldiers anchor one side of the rope, they pull the rope as tight as they can. Next, they tie off the rope using one of three methods: mule knot secured with an overhand knot (see figure 16-1), round turn around anchor and two half hitches on a bight, or a high strength tie off (tensionless hitch). (See figure 16-4, page 374.) Note. Figure 16-2, and figures 16-3 and 16-4, page 374, illustrate the transport tightening system. 16-6. The benefit of hand tensioning the rope is that it is the fastest way to get the rope tight. The limitation is that if the rope bridge span is long, it may not be possible to apply adequate tension to the rope using this method. Adequate tension may require more personnel than units have available. TRANSPORT TIGHTENING SYSTEM 16-7. The transport tightening system can be used to tighten a rope bridge when additional tension is necessary. One Soldier on the near side ties a knot that is easily untied after being placed under tension (for example, an alpine butterfly or figure-eight slip knot with a half

to tighten a rope bridge when additional tension is necessary. One Soldier on the near side ties a knot that is easily untied after being placed under tension (for example, an alpine butterfly or figure-eight slip knot with a half hitch to stabilize the adjustable bight [see figure 16-1]) approximately 1 to 2 meters from the near side anchor. They place a locking carabiner into the loop of the knot. At that time, Soldiers route the remainder of the rope around the near side anchor point and clip the rope into the carabiner. Figure 16-1. Transport tightening system 16-8. The pull team on the near side pulls the slack out of the installation rope. The knot should be close enough to the near side anchor to allow personnel to easily load the installation. 16-9. The benefit of using the transport tightening system is that the MA allows more tension to be applied to the rope with limited personnel and minimal equipment. The limitations are the increased system platform size required, reduced MA due to friction generated by rope redirects, and time of construction. SIMPLE 3:1 TIGHTENING SYSTEM 16-11. Rope Bridges 16-12. The benefits of the simple 3:1 system are increased efficiency in tensioning, the capability to tension on a smaller platform, and the ability to re-tension due to rope stretch. The drawbacks are increased complexity, time, equipment, and the possibility of overtensioning the rope. The limitations are that the system requires more equipment, is more complex to construct, is easier to overtension and the increased time required to construct. WARNING No more than four personnel should be used to tighten the rope when a simple 3:1 or a transport tightening system is used to apply tension. Using more personnel can overtighten the rope and bring the rope critically close to failure. REDUNDANCY 16-13. A rope bridge constructed with a single rope has the risk of critical failure due to cutting and lacks redundancy. A redundancy (in rigging) is the condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of any single component of the system failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge

failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge that is high off the ground, and a dry river crossing where a separate belay rope is not used. If two ropes are used, they should be as close as possible so that a single carabiner can be clipped to both lines. An individual would attach to both ropes when crossing, thus having a backup in case of failure. Redundancy is not always necessary or practical but is typically used in training as a risk management tool. METHODS OF CROSSING 16-14. All wet crossing techniques using handlines are covered in chapter 13. Methods of dry crossings using rope bridges is determined by several factors: * The load being transported on the rope bridge (such as personnel, equipment, and litter). * The risk of the terrain (such as fast-moving water and catastrophic falls). * The angle of the rope bridge (such as level, ascending, and descending). * Equipment available (such as extra ropes, harnesses, and rigging equipment). 16-15. Leaders must evaluate

The risk of the terrain (such as fast-moving water and catastrophic falls). * The angle of the rope bridge (such as level, ascending, and descending). * Equipment available (such as extra ropes, harnesses, and rigging equipment). 16-15. Leaders must evaluate the situation and determine the most efficient means of crossing. For example, the method chosen for moving a light element with no sustainment gear across a 10-foot stream is different from the method chosen for moving crew-served weapons across a 50-foot-wide, fast-moving river. 16-16. If Soldiers can transport themselves across, they can choose either the commando crawl or the Tyrolean traverse. COMMANDO CRAWL 16-17. Soldiers lie on top of the rope with a foot hooked on the rope and a knee bent, o positioned nearly in line with the buttocks; the other leg hangs straight to maintain balance. They progress by pulling with their arms. To recover if they fall over, Soldiers hook one leg and the opposite arm over the rope, and then push down with the other hand to regain position. TYROLEAN TRAVERSE 16-18. Soldiers don a harness or tie a field expedient harness and attach a locking carabiner into it, with the nose of the carabiner facing

the rope, and then push down with the other hand to regain position. TYROLEAN TRAVERSE 16-18. Soldiers don a harness or tie a field expedient harness and attach a locking carabiner into it, with the nose of the carabiner facing up and away from their body. They then face the rope and clip into the rope bridge. Soldiers rotate under the rope and pull with their hands and arms to make progress. The Tyrolean traverse is the preferred method. If crossing with rucksacks, a carabiner is inserted into the frame and attached to the rope bridge. Soldiers then place one or both legs through the shoulder carrying straps and pull the rucksack across. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 375

Chapter 16 TAGLINES 16-19. Heavy equipment will require the use of a tagline. A tagline is used to pull objects from the near side to the far side. An additional rope is brought across the rope bridge and anchored to the far side. The other end is anchored on the near side. All the slack is pulled to the near side, and a figure eight on a bight knot is tied at the loading platform. A carabiner is inserted into the loop and clipped onto the rope bridge. 16-20. If the rope bridge is longer than half a rope length, two separate ropes are required to create a tagline. One end of the far-side tagline is brought across the obstacle and anchored to the far side. The other end is secured to a carabiner. One end of the near side tagline is secured at the near side, and the other end is secured into the same carabiner as the far-side tagline. That carabiner is then placed onto the rope bridge. 16-21. If the rope bridge is descending (the far-side anchor is significantly lower than the near side), a belay may need to be added to the tagline system. The tagline

tagline. That carabiner is then placed onto the rope bridge. 16-21. If the rope bridge is descending (the far-side anchor is significantly lower than the near side), a belay may need to be added to the tagline system. A unit SOP may dictate the rigging of these items, but many expedient methods exist. The rigging should use various items that would be readily available to a deployed unit. Some of these items include tubular nylon webbing, cordage (various sizes), and carabiners. 16-23. lift the bundle for unloading, a releasable Munter mule can be utilized at the point of attachment to the tagline. 16-24. Rope Bridges Figure 16-5. Litter rigging ARTIFICIAL HEIGHT 16-25. Artificial height is often useful or even necessary to raise the height of rope bridges. (See figure 16-6, page 378.) This may be needed when desiring dry river crossings or to better facilitate the loading and unloading of personnel or equipment. Artificial height may be needed on one or both sides of a rope bridge. 16-26. Occasionally, bridge sites may be selected where a tree with a high sturdy limb may be slung with rope or cord. On rock faces, artificial anchors may be constructed in convenient locations. Otherwise, A-frames may need to be constructed. 16-27. A-frames are structures constructed with poles to create artificial height for use with rope bridges. Two sturdy poles are needed. Ensure all knots are removed from both ropes before pulling. HIGH LINES 16-33. A high line is a type of suspended rope bridge used to transport equipment or casualties high above difficult terrain that might otherwise be impassable. These can be used for personnel movement as well, although this is less common. The high line is used over large rivers, ravines, chasms, or diagonally from the top of a cliff to the ground below. The system may be established on different planes, varying from horizontal to near vertical. High lines keep the load suspended above the terrain as it travels directly between the nearand far-side anchors. 16-34. High lines come with a high level of risk due to the height of the load above the ground. High lines used for personnel movement require careful calculation to ensure system failure will not occur, resulting in catastrophic fall injury. They should only be constructed by advanced or master military mountaineers who have been formally trained in high-line construction for this purpose. SITE SELECTION

Appendix A Climbing Route Classification The most important tools for risk management in the mountains are route selection and evaluation. Accurately evaluating and selecting routes in high consequence terrain requires a well-developed understanding of technical route classification systems and experience climbing the terrain they describe. Route classifications allow military mountaineers to identify appropriate routes for their Soldiers' skill levels and the technical rope systems required to move on them safely. Misunderstanding or miscommunicating route difficulty can place the life of the mountaineer or the lives of the Soldiers they lead in danger. The U.S. military does not have its own technical route classification systems. Therefore, military mountaineers must use those developed for civilian mountaineering. The classifications discussed in this chapter breakdown and describe the difficulty associated with routes in various types of terrain. Understanding them provides military mountaineers with the base from which to build route identification and selection experience. ROCK CLIMBING CLASSIFICATIONS A-1. There are several systems for classifying different aspects of rock-climbing difficulty. Different types of climbing require different classifications. Also, skill is not the only factor involved in classifying difficulty. The amount of time and effort necessary to complete a climbing route is often more important than

different aspects of rock-climbing difficulty. Different types of climbing require different classifications. Also, skill is not the only factor involved in classifying difficulty. The amount of time and effort necessary to complete a climbing route is often more important than what the hardest move on it is. Depending on the type of route being planned, one or all these route difficulty systems should be considered. YOSEMITE DECIMAL SYSTEM A-2. In North America, the YDS is used to rate the difficulty of rock-climbing routes. It categorizes terrain according to the techniques and physical difficulties encountered when rock climbing. The YDS classes are- * Class 1-hiking. * Class 2-off-trail scramble with the occasional use of hands. * Class 3-moderate scrambling, with short steps of easy climbing. Ropes may be used for beginners, but a guide can often manage the terrain with good coaching and modeling. * Class 4-simple climbing, with exposure. A rope is often used. A fall could be fatal. * Class 5-rock climbing. Usually requires climbers to rope up, belay, and place protection to protect the leader from a long fall. A-3. Class 5 is further subdivided to rate the difficulty of the climbing. The YDS only rates the hardest

Class 5-rock climbing. Usually requires climbers to rope up, belay, and place protection to protect the leader from a long fall. A-3. Class 5 is further subdivided to rate the difficulty of the climbing. The YDS only rates the hardest move on a pitch and does not account for strenuousness, difficulty of placing protection, or quality of the protection: * Class 5.0 to 5.4-easy. This is the simplest form of free climbing. Hands are necessary to support balance. Easy for experienced climbers. * Class 5.5 to 5.6-intermediate. Often no more physically difficult than easier climbing but requires trusting friction and smaller holds. The climber can experience vertical position or overhangs where there are positive holds that require moderate levels of energy expenditure. * Class 5.7 to 5.8-moderate. Considerable climbing experience is necessary. Longer stretches of climbing requiring several points of intermediate protection. Climbing often requires specific techniques, such as jamming, liebacks, or mantles. * Class 5.9 to 5.10-hard. Requires well above average ability and excellent condition. Exposed positions, often combined with small belay points. Passages of the difficult sections can often be accomplished under good conditions. Often combined with aid climbing. * Class 5.11 to 5.15-very difficult. Requires more climbing

above average ability and excellent condition. Exposed positions, often combined with small belay points. Passages of the difficult sections can often be accomplished under good conditions. Often combined with aid climbing. * Class 5.11 to 5.15-very difficult. Requires more climbing ability, experience, and energy expenditure. Only talented and dedicated climbers reach this level. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 385

It is rated not by the physical difficulty of the climbing but the quality and spacing of the placements for gear: * A0-French-free. No aiders are required. training event. SECTION III - TIME-DISTANCE ESTIMATION B-15. The time-distance method covered in chapter 7, table 7-2, page 148 is useful but very general. The Munter method described below affords planners more options to enhance their time-to-distance estimate. THE MUNTER METHOD B-16. The Munter method is an accurate method of calculating route times during planning. It is the most accepted time-distance formula used by mountain professionals and guides. The Munter method combines map distance (kilometers) and elevation change (meters) into a unit of time (hours), then it is divided by an estimated movement rate (kilometers per hour) using various terrain conditions. This method allows the user the ability to break the movement up into different legs and account for different modes of travel. This method is simple to calculate and allows the planner increased flexibility to account for the various paces, changes in elevation, increased loads, and environmental conditions that exist in mountainous terrain. An advanced military mountaineer has been trained in advanced mountaineering techniques and is also known as a level 2 mountaineer. *aid climbing Climbing technique in which standing on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed protection is used to make upward progress. *assault climber A role assigned to a Soldier or

as a level 2 mountaineer. *aid climbing Climbing technique in which standing on or pulling oneself up via devices attached to fixed or placed protection is used to make upward progress. *assault climber A role assigned to a Soldier or team during tactical operations who is responsible for the location and establishment of technical routes in class 3 or higher terrain; ideally, a level 2 mountaineer. *basic military mountaineer A Soldier who graduated from the Basic Military Mountaineer Course. Basic military mountaineers have been trained in basic mountaineering techniques, such as fundamental mobility skills necessary to move safely and efficiently in mountainous terrain, and are also known as level 1 military mountaineers. *belay A system of using a rope as a backup in steep terrain to arrest a Soldier's fall should one occur. 400 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glossary *bolt A type of rock protection or anchoring component comprised of an expansion bolt or glue-in shaft attached to a hanger to which a carabiner can be attached. *brake strand The strand of a rope system that controls the rate at which a load is lowered or a rappeller descends. carabiner A D-shaped or oval-shaped metal link, with one spring-hinged side, that is used in mountaineering as a connector between soft materials and to capture a freely running rope. *cold-weather injury Any preventable injury resulting from exposure to cold environmental conditions. *coil A secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling. couloir Narrow snow- or ice-filled gully. dynamic rope Kernmantle rope designed to stretch and absorb force, primarily used to protect climbers from fall injuries. fall protection Any anchor clipped to a running rope used in belay systems that limits the distance a roped climber falls, should a fall occur. friction hitch A type of hitch tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily while no force is applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned. guidebook A publication containing detailed climbing routes and approach route information. gully A

tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily while no force is applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned. guidebook A publication containing detailed climbing routes and approach route information. gully A channel caused by erosion, especially by water running down a slope; it is generally narrower and steeper than a draw. hands-free backup A rigging technique, involving friction hitches or mechanical devices that prevent a load from falling should control of a brake strand be lost. hauling system A technical rope system used to move a load up steep or vertical terrain comprised of rigging that generates increased mechanical advantage and captures progress. high-strength tie off A single-point anchoring method that retains maximum installation rope strength and releasability, using multiple-round turns around the anchor object to create friction, and securing the end back to itself ensuring no force is applied to any component knots or carabiners. installation rope The primary load-bearing rope or strand in a rope system. kernmantle rope A rope constructed with a load-bearing core of twisted synthetic fibers and a protective outer sheath of interwoven synthetic fibers. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 401

Glossary knot The fixed portion of a rope that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the process of being tied for some purpose. Sometimes referred to as a "hard knot" since its condition will remain intact until actively untied. *lead climbing Climbing a route while attached to the end of a rope to place devices in rock, ice, or snow for fall protection with a belayer located below. *lead climber The first climber to negotiate a route, for whom a top belay is not possible, and who assumes the most risk of injury in a fall. *load management The act or strategy of planning and packing loads to reduce negative impacts on Soldier physical performance. *lowering system A technical rope system used to move a load down steep or vertical terrain in a controlled fashion using friction hitches or mechanical devices. *master military mountaineer A Soldier extensively trained and experienced with mountaineering techniques who the commander appoints to serve as a subject matter expert. Master military mountaineers are graduates of the Basic Military Mountaineer Course and Advanced Military Mountaineer Course. They possess all the skills of the advanced military mountaineer and have extensive practical experience in

They possess all the skills of the advanced military mountaineer and have extensive practical experience in a variety of mountain environments in both winter and summer conditions. *mechanical advantage Reduction in the force required to move a load, which comes at the cost of time and distance. Specific rope rigging techniques in mountaineering generate mechanical advantage. multipoint anchor More than one fixed object joined with technical rigging to form an anchor system capable of suspending the weight or arresting the fall of an attached load. natural anchor A natural fixed object (such as a tree, rock formation, or ice formation) to which a rope system can be secured, and is of sufficient size, weight, and security to suspend the weight of or arrest the fall of an attached load. pitch A section of a climb that comprises the distance between two belay stations, which can be up to a standard rope length (60 meters). prolonged field care The continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care.

(JP 4-02) redundancy (in rigging) The condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of any single component of the system failing. safety knot A backup knot tied to prevent a primary knot from slipping loose. scrambling The act of moving over difficult or broken terrain, characterized by using mostly walking techniques but requires some use of the hands for balance or other specific climbing techniques. 402 TC 3-97.61 26 November 2025

Glossary self-equalizing anchor A multipoint anchor comprised of adjustable strands from each anchor component to a shared attachment point that allows for maximum load sharing even when direction of pull changes during use. *simul-climbing A belay technique involving two Soldiers climbing simultaneously while attached to the ends of a rope which runs through the fall protection. snowpack The entire mass of snow covering a given area of terrain. static rope Kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling, lowering, and anchor systems construction. *technical route A route through steep or broken mountainous terrain that presents significant risk of fall injury and requires special movement techniques or ropes to ensure adequate safety for Soldiers moving through it. *vertical danger area Steep terrain that significantly restricts a unit's ability to maneuver, thereby putting the unit at significant tactical disadvantage should enemy contact be made while moving through the VDA. 26 November 2025 TC 3-97.61 403

EMERGENCY DISINFECTION OF DRINKING WATER In an emergency situation where regular water service has been interrupted - like a hurricane, flood, or water pipe breakage - local authorities may recommend using only bottled water, boiled water, or disinfected water until regular water service is restored. The instructions below show you how to boil and disinfect water to kill most disease-causing microorganisms that may be present in the water. However, boiling or disinfection will not destroy other contaminants, such as heavy metals, salts, and most other chemicals. ONLY USE WATER THAT HAS BEEN PROPERLY DISINFECTED FOR DRINKING, COOKING, MAKING ANY PREPARED DRINK, WASHING DISHES, AND FOR BRUSHING TEETH. Use bottled water or water you have properly prepared and stored as an emergency water supply. Boil water, if you do not have bottled water. Boiling is sufficient to kill pathogenic bacteria, viruses and protozoa (WHO, 2015). - If water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter. - Bring water to a rolling boil for at least one minute. At altitudes above 5,000 feet (1,000 meters), boil water for three minutes. - Let water cool naturally and store it in clean containers with

towel, or coffee filter. - Bring water to a rolling boil for at least one minute. At altitudes above 5,000 feet (1,000 meters), boil water for three minutes. - Let water cool naturally and store it in clean containers with covers. - To improve the flat taste of boiled water, add one pinch of salt to each quart or liter of water, or pour the water from one clean container to another several times. Disinfect water using household bleach, if you can't boil water. Only use regular, unscented chlorine bleach products that are suitable for disinfection and sanitization as indicated on the label. The label may say that the active ingredient contains 6 or 8.25% of sodium hypochlorite. Do not use scented, color safe, or bleaches with added cleaners. - If water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter. - Locate a clean dropper from your medicine cabinet or emergency supply kit. - Locate a fresh liquid chlorine bleach or liquid chlorine bleach that is stored at room temperatures for less than one year. - Use the table on the next page as a guide to decide how much bleach

Backer et al. Page 3 Author Manuscript Etiology and Risk of Waterborne Infection WILDERNESS SETTINGS Author Manuscript Millions of people enter wilderness areas each year and drink surface water. Even in developed countries with low rates of diarrheal illness, regular waterborne disease outbreaks indicate that the microbiologic quality of the water, especially surface water, is not ensured.4-7 Public health agencies regularly report outbreaks of disease associated with surface water from backcountry and parks as well as from campground water systems. The environment and activity upstream from the travelers' surface water source defines the risk. Side streams draining springs, snowmelt, and glaciers where there is no human or animal activity are lower risk. In contrast, upstream usage by humans, farm animals, or wildlife pose a major risk. Cattle excrete pathogenic strains of Escherichia coli and Salmonella and have been found in multiple studies to be the major animal species contributing to waterborne disease in North America.8,9 Giardiasis is a zoonotic infection with numerous host species, including farm animals, deer and other wild ungulates, beavers, and even household animals; however, the extent of transmission to humans is less defined.10 Nonalpine wilderness areas in the United States may have streams and rivers that

with numerous host species, including farm animals, deer and other wild ungulates, beavers, and even household animals; however, the extent of transmission to humans is less defined.10 Nonalpine wilderness areas in the United States may have streams and rivers that are contaminated with animal waste, including farm animal runoff, or may be contaminated with incompletely treated sewage from towns and urban areas. Page 5 Author Manuscript Author Manuscript The term disinfection, the desired result of field water treatment, is used here to indicate the removal or destruction of harmful microorganisms, which reduces the risk of illness. This is sometimes used interchangeably with purification, but the latter term more accurately indicates the removal of organic or inorganic chemicals and particulate matter to improve color, taste, and odor. Unless specifically designed to remove chemical contaminants, disinfection techniques may not make water safe from chemical exposures. Potable implies drinkable water, but it technically means that a water source, on average, over a period of time, contains a minimal microbial hazard so that the statistical likelihood of illness is acceptably low. All standards, including water regulations in the United States, acknowledge the impracticality of trying to eliminate all microorganisms from drinking water. Generally, the goal is a 3 to 5 log reduction (99.9-99.999%), allowing a small risk of enteric infection. Most microorganisms, especially protozoan cysts, also settle eventually, but this takes much longer.33 Simply allowing the water to sit undisturbed for about 1 h or until sediment has formed on the bottom of the container and then decanting or filtering the clear water from the top through a coffee filter or finely woven cloth will remove many larger particles from the water. a routine step in municipal water treatment.34,35 C-F can remove smaller suspended particles and chemical complexes too small to settle by gravity (colloids). Coagulation is achieved with the addition of a chemical that causes particles to stick together by electrostatic and ionic forces. Flocculation is a physical process that promotes the formation of larger particles by gentle mixing. Alum (an aluminum salt), lime (alkaline chemicals principally containing calcium or magnesium with oxygen), or iron salts are commonly used coagulants. Backer et al. Page 8 Author Manuscript Disinfection Methods HEAT Heat is the oldest and most reliable means of water disinfection. Heat inactivation of microorganisms is a function of time and temperature (exponential function of first-order kinetics). Thus, the thermal death point is reached in a shorter time at higher temperatures, whereas lower temperatures are effective if applied for a longer time. Pasteurization uses this principle to kill food pathogens and spoiling organisms at temperatures well below boiling, generally between 60°C (140°F) and 70°C (158°F). Flash pasteurization occurs within 30 s at 70 to 72°C (158 to 162°F).48,49 Author Manuscript All common enteric pathogens are readily inactivated by heat at pasteurization temperatures, although microorganisms vary in heat sensitivity, with protozoan cysts being the most sensitive to heat, bacteria intermediate, and viruses less sensitive (Table 1 50-62).50,51 Only bacterial spores are more resistant, but they are not generally enteric pathogens.52 As enteric pathogens are killed within seconds by boiling water rapidly at temperatures > 60°C (140°F), the traditional advice to boil water for 10 min to ensure potable water is excessive. The time required to heat water from 55°C (131°F) to aboil works toward disinfection; therefore, any water brought to a

at temperatures > 60°C (140°F), the traditional advice to boil water for 10 min to ensure potable water is excessive. The time required to heat water from 55°C (131°F) to aboil works toward disinfection; therefore, any water brought to a rapid boil should be adequately disinfected.63 Boiling for 1 min is recommended by the US CDC to account for user variability in identifying boiling points and adds a margin of safety. The boiling point decreases with increasing altitude, but this is not significant compared with the time required for thermal death at these temperatures (Table 2). Author Manuscript Improvisational techniques-In wilderness or travel environments, the main limitation for using heat is availability of fuel. Although attaining boiling temperature is not necessary to kill microorganisms, boiling is the only easily recognizable endpoint without use of a thermometer. Based on microbiologic testing, hot tap water has been proposed as a means of heat disinfection.64,65 Most water from hot water taps measured in countries outside the United States measured 55 to 60°C (131 to 140°F).51 As a rule of thumb, water too hot to touch fell within the pasteurization range, but tolerance to touch is too variable to be reliable.66 Author Manuscript If

However, this improvisational measure is less useful for hotels that use on-demand water heaters without a hot water tank. Travelers with access to electricity can boil water with either a small electric heating coil or a lightweight electric beverage warmer brought from home.
